articles.body:
President Trump marked Election Day by issuing two proclamations on space and anti-communism Tuesday.

The president signed “the American Declaration of Freedom in Space,” which states Earth’s solar system and outer space “are open to exploration, development, use, and the establishment of a permanent presence” by U.S. citizens.

A second proclamation Trump signed declared Nov. 1-7 “Anti-communism Week.”

“I call upon all Americans to stand firm in their defense against any threat to the American way of life and to protect our burning flame of liberty from the darkness of communism,” Trump said in the proclamation.

The announcement of the proclamations comes as the first polls close on Election Day.

Polls show Trump and Republicans facing an uphill climb in their battle to defend their majorities in the House and the Senate as Democrats hammer Republicans over the administration’s handling of affordability and the economy.

“The President has left it all out on the field and he’s done everything that was needed. Republicans are in a better spot now than they were four weeks ago,” a White House official told The Hill.

Trump is expected to watch the results come in during an election watch party in the White House East Room Tuesday evening.

articles.title: Mullin slams Hillary Clinton for poll intimidation warning
articles.summary: Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Tuesday dismissed a warning from former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton this week that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers could try to intimidate voters at the polls. “I don’t understand why Hillary is still relevant,” Mullin told Fox News host Will Cain ahead of election…
articles.body:
Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Tuesday dismissed a warning from former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton this week that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers could try to intimidate voters at the polls.

“I don’t understand why Hillary is still relevant,” Mullin told Fox News host Will Cain ahead of election night.

On the Monday show of ABC’s “The View,” Clinton referenced the Trump administration’s recent legal fights with states over their election processes and suggested the DHS could send federal agents to the polls.

“What I do think they’re trying to do in some places is intimidation,” she said. “You know, having ICE or others show up and just be standing there, staring at people, looking threatening to voters coming in to vote. But I do think, you know, people are tougher than that.”

Clinton said she spoke Sunday with Rep. Joe Morelle (D-N.Y.), who is leading the Democratic Party’s election integrity response efforts. The former secretary of State said any attempts by the Trump administration to intimidate voters “won’t go unanswered.”

Mullin brushed off Clinton’s warning about ICE officers at the polls, noting Democrats have been “pushing this narrative” for several months.

“Even in my confirmation hearing, this was brought up, and I made it very clear that ICE agents aren’t going to be around polling places unless there’s a threat,” the secretary said.

“The only reason you’d see the Department of Homeland Security is if there’s a threat that we have to be responding to, not to try to intimidate or be around a polling place,” he continued. “That’s not their job. We’re enforcing immigration.”

Morelle responded to Clinton’s comments in a social media post on Election Day.

“Secretary @HillaryClinton is right: We won’t let threats to our elections go unanswered,” he wrote in the post. “Americans should have every confidence as they cast their votes today.”

On Tuesday, the Department of Justice (DOJ) announced it had deployed Election Day monitors to all 50 U.S. states in its “largest monitoring effort in history.”

Local Democratic leaders decried the move, with Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass (D) calling it a “baseless and dangerous attack” on state election processes.

President Trump and his administration have repeatedly warned about vulnerabilities in the election system, as Republicans fight to retain their control of Congress in the midterm elections.

On Friday, a federal judge ordered the DOJ not to threaten or intimidate election officials ahead of the midterm elections, after the department sent letters to election officials in California and Washington, requesting they separate out any ballots identified by the federal government as potential noncitizens.

Additionally, a federal judge on Sunday dismissed the Trump administration’s lawsuit in Alaska that sought to block the certification of the state’s Senate race if Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) loses his reelection bid.

The administration had argued the Democratic challenger’s campaign’s reported efforts to recruit a spoiler candidate with the same name as the incumbent senator were an attempt to mislead voters who would vote for the senator. Despite the ruling, Republicans are already organizing a “recount refund” for the race, according to a Tuesday filing with the Federal Election Commission.

articles.body:
Democrats eye investigations of Trump’s DC projects

If Democrats take back one or both chambers, they’ll unlock a sweeping new set of investigative powers they could unleash on President Trump’s D.C. projects.

For months, Democrats have lamented the Trump administration’s efforts to “beautify” Washington, D.C., including construction on the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, plans to build an arch near Arlington National Cemetery and efforts to build a White House ballroom.

While the party out of power has attempted to investigate these and additional Trump activities during the president’s first two years in office, getting control of Congress would also mean that Democrats would be able to demand documents and subpoena witnesses — powers they could use to take Trump and his allies to task.

“We’re going to be making up for two years of zero oversight by this feckless MAGA Congress, and on top of that, we’re going to have to tackle everything that pops up on our watch,” Rep. Jared Huffman (Calif.), the top Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, told The Hill on Monday.

Ahead of the nation’s 250th birthday, the Trump administration embarked on several contentious projects , including renovations to the Reflecting Pool and the creation of a White House ballroom.

The projects included a series of contracts that, contrary to ordinary procedure, were awarded through a no-bid process, meaning they were awarded to one firm without an open process for other companies to make competing offers.

The New York Times reported that some of the projects included inflated profit margins for the contractors.

“A lot of this is no-bid contracts that just have the stench of corruption and self-dealing and incompetence, and we deserve better than a government that operates that way, so we’re going to just shine a bright light, and there is a sanitizing effect of even that,” Huffman said.

articles.title: DOJ sends target letters in Alaska probe to 20 Democrats
articles.summary: The Department of Justice (DOJ) has sent letters to 20 Democrats informing them they are being looked at as part of an investigation into ballot-stacking in Alaska, The New York Times reported Tuesday. DOJ officials informed recipients that they may be targets of an investigation or asked them to preserve records over the effort to…
articles.body:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) has sent letters to 20 Democrats informing them they are being looked at as part of an investigation into ballot-stacking in Alaska, The New York Times reported Tuesday .

DOJ officials informed recipients that they may be targets of an investigation or asked them to preserve records over the effort to get a candidate with the same name as Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan (Alaska) on the ballot this November.

The Trump administration has moved to block certification of the Senate election if candidate Dan J. Sullivan causes the incumbent to lose to former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska).

The DOJ has historically avoided taking action that involves elections so close to Election Day but has not followed the precedent during President Trump’s second term. The Times reported that the DOJ is investigating possible donor fraud and conspiracy charges related to Democrats’ alleged effort to recruit the second Sullivan candidate to run for Senate.

Republicans and DOJ officials have said they believe the existence of the second Sullivan on the ballot may amount to a deliberate attempt to confuse voters and throw the election to Peltola. Both parties have legally practiced ballot-stacking for decades, but in this case, Trump has publicly pushed the DOJ to hold those involved “ criminally responsible .”

Peltola and Democratic officials have denied they had any involvement with the other Sullivan’s run for Senate despite the Times reporting that he was recruited directly by Democratic operatives.

Democratic lawyer Marc Elias is reportedly one of the recipients of the letters after Trump recently advocated for his prosecution . Elias said in a statement that he is being targeted by a “weaponized” DOJ that is pursuing the president’s political enemies despite “zero evidence” of wrongdoing. Trump said Elias should “go to jail” in an appearance on Fox News .

“We will not be intimidated by a sham investigation. We are going to keep working around the clock to support our clients and make sure President Trump and his party enjoy a well-deserved beating at the ballot box,” Elias said.

DDHQ projected Warner as the winner with zero percent of the vote reported shortly after polls closed at 7 p.m. EST.

Warner has served in the upper chamber since 2009 and is the vice chair of the Senate’s Select Committee on Intelligence. The incumbent is also a vice chair of the Senate Democratic Caucus.

The Democrat previously served as governor of the Old Dominion from 2002-06. A Republican has not been elected to the Senate in the state since 2002.

Warner is the wealthiest Democratic senator, per Investopedia , with a net worth of more than $200 million. Before entering politics, he was a venture capitalist and tech entrepreneur.

articles.title: Early exit polls: 38 percent approve of Trump, lower than past 4 presidents
articles.summary: Early exit polls from CBS News on Tuesday found that just 38 percent of respondents approved of President Trump — notably fewer than exit polling during midterm cycles in his first term and the terms of the previous three presidents. The approval rating was also lower than exit polling in 2006 when only 43 percent…
articles.body:
Early exit polls from CBS News on Tuesday found that just 38 percent of respondents approved of President Trump — notably fewer than exit polling during midterm cycles in his first term and the terms of the previous three presidents.

The approval rating was also lower than exit polling in 2006 when only 43 percent of voters approved of then-President George W. Bush, the same year he lost both chambers of Congress.

The CBS News survey also found that 59 percent of respondents said the president factored into their midterm vote for the House.

When asked how they felt about the United States currently, only 7 percent reported feeling enthusiastic compared to 18 percent who said satisfied, 37 percent who said dissatisfied and 38 percent who said angry.

When it came to political parties, 46 percent of respondents held a favorable opinion of Democrats compared to 54 percent who didn’t. For the GOP, 41 percent had a favorable view of the party, while 59 percent held an unfavorable one.

Trump and the GOP’s approval ratings have tanked in recent months amid growing concern over the cost of living.

CNN’s preliminary national results found that roughly 75 percent of respondents said they felt dissatisfied or worse with the way things are going in the country. Their analysis noted this was driven by negative views of Trump and dissatisfaction with current economic conditions.

Six in 10 respondents nationally disapproved of the president’s job performance in the poll as well.

articles.title: Schwartzel wins Florida House seat vacated by Donalds
articles.summary: Republican Jim Schwartzel is projected to win Florida’s 19th District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Byron Donalds (R-Fla.), who gave up his seat to run for…
articles.body:
Republican Jim Schwartzel is projected to win Florida’s 19th District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Schwartzel defeated Democrat Victor Arias, keeping a GOP stronghold in southwest Florida firmly in Republican hands. The victory sends the conservative media executive to Washington to replace Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.), who gave up his seat to run for governor .

He emerged from a crowded Republican primary in August that featured several prominent candidates, including two former members of Congress seeking political comebacks . Among them were former Reps. Chris Collins (R-N.Y.) and Madison Cawthorn (R-N.C.), along with former Illinois state Sen. Jim Oberweis.

But Schwartzel’s biggest primary victory came against Catalina Lauf, a conservative activist who had secured President Trump’s endorsement.

The GOP front-runner captured roughly 29 percent of the primary vote, compared with Lauf’s 22 percent, marking a setback for the president.

DDHQ ranked the race as a “safe Republican” seat heading into Election Day. Schwartzel led Arias 58.7 percent to 40.2 percent with 76 percent of the vote reported by DDHQ as of 7:23 p.m. EST Tuesday.

A longtime southwest Florida resident and radio station owner, Schwartzel emphasized his local roots throughout the campaign, contrasting his ties to the region with opponents who had previously sought office elsewhere. The district includes portions of Lee and Collier counties.

He also entered the final stretch with a substantial fundraising advantage over Arias, raising roughly $2.8 million compared with less than $70,000 for the Democrat, according to filings from the Federal Election Commission.

articles.title: Clark wins Georgia House race to replace late David Scott
articles.summary: Democrat Jasmine Clark is projected to win the race to represent Georgia’s 13th District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Clark defeated Republican Jonathan Chavez with over 81 percent of the vote at 58 percent of ballots counted, securing a victory in the blue district outside Atlanta. The win sends the Georgia state lawmaker and…
articles.body:
Democrat Jasmine Clark is projected to win the race to represent Georgia’s 13th District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Clark defeated Republican Jonathan Chavez with over 81 percent of the vote at 58 percent of ballots counted, securing a victory in the blue district outside Atlanta.

The win sends the Georgia state lawmaker and microbiologist to Washington, succeeding the late Rep. David Scott (D-Ga.), who died in April after more than two decades in Congress.

Clark, who has served in the Georgia House since 2019, emerged from a crowded Democratic primary in May, winning more than 56 percent of the vote and avoiding a runoff contest.

Her Democratic primary opponents included former Gwinnett County school board chair Everton Blair, Georgia state Sen. Emanuel Jones (D) and Heavenly Kimes, a dentist and reality TV personality known for appearing on Bravo’s “Married to Medicine.”

Scott’s death dramatically reshaped the contest, which initially featured several Democrats seeking to unseat the longtime incumbent.

Blair ultimately won a separate special election in August to serve the remainder of Scott’s term, defeating the late lawmaker’s daughter , Marcye Scott, in a runoff. But he was not on the November ballot.

Clark faced Chavez, a 23-year Air Force veteran and radiologist who ran unopposed in the Republican primary.

DDHQ rated the race “safe Democratic” heading into Election Day.

A scientist by training, Clark holds a doctorate in microbiology and molecular genetics from Emory University, where she serves as an assistant clinical professor in the nursing school.

She first won election to the Georgia Legislature in 2018, flipping a Republican-held seat in the Atlanta suburbs.

During her time in the state House, the Democrat has emerged as a vocal advocate for abortion rights, public health and education. On the campaign trail, Clark emphasized her scientific background while criticizing President Trump’s policies, particularly on healthcare.

articles.title: Gilbert wins election to succeed Florida’s Wilson in House
articles.summary: Democrats easily retained their hold on Florida’s 24th District on Tuesday when Oliver Gilbert, a local county official, defeated Republican Tedora Brown in the race to replace retiring Rep. Frederica Wilson (D-Fla.), Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) projects. The contest was never close. The district, which encompasses parts of northern Miami, consists overwhelmingly of Black and Hispanic…
articles.body:
Democrats easily retained their hold on Florida’s 24th District on Tuesday when Oliver Gilbert, a local county official, defeated Republican Tedora Brown in the race to replace retiring Rep. Frederica Wilson (D-Fla.), Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) projects.

The contest was never close. The district, which encompasses parts of northern Miami, consists overwhelmingly of Black and Hispanic voters, who tend to support Democrats. The Republicans’ redistricting efforts this year altered the lines of the 24th District a bit but without making it competitive. Former Vice President Kamala Harris carried the district by 39 points in 2024.

Gilbert took 83.8 percent of the vote to Brown’s 17.2 percent, with 61 percent of the vote reported by DDHQ as of 7:21 p.m. EST on Tuesday.

Gilbert’s victory in the deep blue district was all but assured after his primary win in August, when he bested a crowded Democratic primary field that included Kendrick Meek Jr., whose father and grandmother had both represented the district in the House.

Gilbert, Miami-Dade County commissioner and a former mayor of Miami Gardens, got a big boost in the form of an endorsement from Wilson, a former educator who has served in Congress for 16 years. Wilson, who will turn 84 on Thursday, announced her retirement in May, saying it was time to pass the torch to a younger generation of lawmakers.

“Even leather wears out,” she said at the time.

Brown, a self-described businesswoman and real estate developer, had initially run this year as a Republican in Illinois’s 11th District, which is represented by Democratic Rep. Bill Foster. She lost the GOP primary with less than 6 percent of the vote before jumping to Florida to vie for Wilson’s seat.

Brown’s campaign was dogged by allegations that she and her husband had skimmed almost $750,000 in COVID-19 relief funding for personal purchases, including items at Tiffany & Co. and Saks Fifth Avenue. Her husband pleaded guilty, while Brown is fighting the charges.

articles.title: Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff cruises to re-election in Georgia
articles.summary: Ossoff defeated GOP Rep. Mike Collins, NBC News projects, after a race in which his speeches drew national attention from Democrats looking for future party leaders.
articles.body: Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff has won re-election against Republican Rep. Mike Collins, NBC News projects, prevailing in Georgia after a nationally watched race that was defined, at times, by heated personal attacks. Ossoff’s win is a major hold for Democrats in one of the most closely divided battleground states in the country — and one that both sides saw as critical for control of the Senate earlier this election cycle. Ossoff grabbed an early advantage in the race and held on, with a massive money advantage and a sizable lead in most public polling. In a victory speech Tuesday night, Ossoff told supporters that “the American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption, and incompetence of the failed lame duck President Donald J. Trump.” Striking a different note, he also thanked Republican mayors and leaders who backed him during the campaign, as well as the Republican and independent voters who joined his coalition. “Never doubt that unity is possible,” Ossoff said. His dominant position in a state where both parties have won in recent years turned heads nationally, and clips of Ossoff’s campaign speeches began to catch on among national Democrats throughout 2026. Follow live updates on the midterm elections That prompted some talk of whether Ossoff could run for president in 2028, though he said during a debate that he would serve a full second term. Much of the race, including two head-to-head debates, focused on the national political atmosphere, with Ossoff tying Collins to Trump and his low approval rating. Meanwhile, Collins would often try to pivot to votes Ossoff took under former Democratic President Joe Biden, who left office in January 2025. The economy and the increasingly high price of consumer goods were also at the center of the race. Ossoff repeatedly tried to get Collins to defend Trump’s tariff regime and the Iran war. Collins would regularly try to brush off questions about Trump’s economy, including the tariffs, and instead try to blame Biden-era policies for high costs. “That Bidenomics, that Green New Deal my opponent voted for, that’s where this inflation came from,” Collins said at their first Senate debate. The race also was replete with attacks of a more personal nature. Ossoff focused on a series of social media posts in which Collins’ son-in-law promoted white nationalist posts, as well as a former Collins staffer’s messages with avowed white supremacist Nick Fuentes. “You’ve hired half the Third Reich,” Ossoff said at a debate last month. Collins said he doesn’t support any form of racism or white nationalism. “I don’t care where the source is, and I tell him that,” Collins said of his son-in-law. Collins also noted campaign contributions to a pro-Ossoff super PAC from Reid Hoffman, a billionaire whose name appeared in the Epstein files. Ossoff retorted that Collins had taken votes to block full release of the files. As Trump’s approval ratings continued to drop, Republicans across the country started to try to distance themselves from him, including rebranding their messaging or finding individual policies to start disagreeing with, most notably tariffs and the war in Iran, both of which are overwhelmingly unpopular. Collins, however, wasn’t one of them. He defended the war in Iran, promoting the administration’s rationale that it’s needed because Iran can’t be allowed to have a nuclear weapon. He said the tariffs were “fair” in the context of the state’s major ports and trade with China. “Savannah Port and Brunswick Port have been on my mind,” Collins said in a debate last month.

articles.title: Trump admin puts alleged 'Decoy Dan' conspirators on notice in Alaska election spoiler probe
articles.summary: The Justice Department has issued more than 120 subpoenas and 20 target letters in its probe of Daniel J. Sullivan's Alaska Senate candidacy.
articles.body: The Justice Department sent out more than 20 target and preservation letters as part of its investigation into Daniel J. Sullivan’s campaign for U.S. Senate in Alaska, two sources familiar with the investigation told Fox News Digital. President Donald Trump's DOJ launched in July its investigation into the retired schoolteacher suspected of being recruited as a spoiler candidate in the race against Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, earning him the nickname "Decoy Dan." 2026 MIDTERM ELECTION DAY RESULTS: LIVE UPDATES A source familiar with the investigation said more than 120 subpoenas have been issued since the probe began this summer. The investigation initially focused on whether Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy was intended to confuse voters and undermine the fairness of the election. "This is a situation where everybody agrees that there is a FRAUD on the ballot," Attorney General Todd Blanche told Fox News Digital. "Everybody agrees that there is a man running that doesn't want to run, that doesn't expect to be senator, that is only running to confuse Alaskan voters." TIM SCOTT DECLARES ALLEGED 'DECOY DAN' PLOT A 'CRIMINAL OFFENSE' AS DOJ INVESTIGATION ROCKS ALASKA Last Thursday, the Trump administration issued more than 30 subpoenas in a 24-hour period following a New York Times report detailing alleged coordination between the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, Democratic operatives and people connected to Mary Peltola’s campaign to recruit Sullivan, a source familiar told Fox News Digital. The New York Times first reported on Election Day that the Justice Department had issued the letter notifying individuals that they were under investigation and letters notifying individuals to preserve their communications and documentations. The report named Marc Elias, an election lawyer whose firm Elias Law Group has represented Peltola, and an official from the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, as recipients of those notices. It is not clear who else has received comment preservation or target letters. TRUMP PROSECUTIONS UNDER BIDEN SET PRECEDENT FOR DOJ’S ALASKA ‘DECOY DAN’ PROBE, EX-FEC CHAIR SAYS President Trump has been highly critical of the alleged efforts of the Democratic Party to siphon voters away from Sen. Sullivan. His administration previously filed a lawsuit against Alaska officials to prevent them from certifying election results if it was deemed Daniel J. Sullivan may have cost Sen. Sullivan the election. That that lawsuit was tossed out by a federal judge Sunday. DOJ FACES ‘HEAVY LIFT’ IN ALASKA ELECTION APPEAL AS SEPARATE CRIMINAL PROBE CONTINUES "You had the Democrat Party headed up by Elias, their lawyer, who was a bad guy, very bad guy — should go to jail, in my opinion," Trump shared on "Fox & Friends Tuesday." "But you had the Democrat Party look all over Alaska for somebody named Sullivan." Trump also suggested that Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer should be held "criminally responsible," as well. Sources familiar with the investigation shared with Fox News Digital that the letters were not sent exclusively to Democratic officials, but they would not give more information or provide specifics about who the recipients were or how many received target versus preservation letters. The letters were not sent out on Election Day. Alaska Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy argued this the state's nonpartisan primary system is to blame for allowing Daniel J. Sullivan to advance to the general election. Under Alaskan's election system, the top four finishers regardless of their party will advance. Daniel J. Sullivan did not run under any political party. "If this was a historical primary, a primary that our fathers and grandfathers had, this individual [retired schoolteacher Dan Sullivan of Petersburg] would not have gotten out of the primary," Dunleavy told Fox News Digital. The heightened focus in the Alaskan Senate race comes after the New York Times investigation last week, which followed with Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman officially announcing at a news conference Friday the investigation into Daniel J. Sullivan's campaign. Heyman did not say at the news conference what criminal charges are being pursued. The Justice Department declined to comment on the ongoing investigation when reached by Fox News Digital. Fox News' Charles Creitz contributed to this report.

articles.title: Paper ballot shortages spark Election Day scramble at polling places in several states
articles.summary: Election Day saw ballot shortages in Kansas, Illinois and Maryland Tuesday, and one voter said the disruption feels like voter suppression.
articles.body: Voters in multiple states encountered paper ballot shortages on Election Day Tuesday, and some left polling places without casting ballots as election officials scrambled to address disruptions during the high-stakes 2026 midterms. Ballot shortages were reported at polling locations in Illinois, Kansas and Maryland as voters headed to the polls Tuesday. In Linwood, Kansas, where voters were casting ballots in a closely watched Senate race as Republicans fight to maintain control of the chamber, a ballot shortage forced some voters to leave their polling place without casting a ballot after election officials failed to provide enough ballots to meet demand. TRUMP-BACKED SENATOR ADMITS GOP FACES NIGHTMARE SCENARIO IN STATE REPUBLICANS HAVEN'T LOST IN 90 YEARS One voter told the Kansas Reflector that her 18-year-old son left without voting after officials ran out of paper ballots. She said she saw another 10 to 15 people leave without casting ballots. Leavenworth County said in a press release the ballot shortage occurred due to an error in the number of ballots ordered. "The shortage was discovered early, and efforts to correct the mistake began immediately. We recognize the importance of ensuring that every eligible voter has the opportunity to cast a ballot. We sincerely apologize for this mistake and any inconvenience or concern it may have caused," the press release said. FLORIDA POLLING PLACES IN 7 COUNTIES ARE MOVING LOCATIONS DUE TO FLOODING "The number of ballots needed was 1,000, the polling station received only 100. The situation has since been remedied since early this morning, and voters are able to vote," the Kansas Secretary of State communications spokesperson told Fox News Digital. In Chicago, voters encountered ballot shortages at several polling locations, prompting election officials to deliver additional ballots and direct voters to alternative voting centers, according to ABC7 Chicago. "There are several precincts for which the board is printing and delivering extra paper ballots and possible extra touch-screen voting machines. As far as we know, no voters have been turned away or unable to vote," the Chicago Board of Elections told the outlet. "It's not unusual for an election authority to have to supply additional ballots to a polling place if turnout is higher than anticipated," Illinois State Board of Elections Public Information Officer Matt Dietrich told Fox News Digital. "We've heard from voters that there are lines at some Chicago polling places but, again, that's not out of the ordinary in a general election." In Brandywine, Maryland, voters faced long lines and delays Tuesday after Brandywine Elementary School, a polling location in Prince George’s County, ran out of paper ballots, according to local outlet WJLA. The school did not have correct ballots, which were later corrected, Prince George’s County Board of Elections Administrator Wendy Honesty-Bey told local outlet The Banner. THE BATTLE FOR CONGRESS IS JUST THE BEGINNING. HERE'S WHAT'S AT STAKE ON ELECTION DAY "The State Board of Election's (SBE) mission is to ensure voting occurs. We, of course, conduct lessons learned after every election and will do so after this election. Once made aware of this situation, more ballots and supplies were deployed to the polling place," an SBE spokesperson told Fox News Digital. While ballot shortages may be gripping some polling precincts, voting machines in Westchester County, New York, are rejecting paper ballots at polling locations throughout the county. "However, Election Day machines elsewhere in the county continued to use the original programming and therefore could not recognize and accept the ballots being used for Election Day."

articles.title: Democrat Jon Ossoff wins re-election to Senate in Georgia
articles.summary: Ossoff is seen as a potential leading contender for the Democratic nomination for president in 2028 if he throws his hat in the ring.
articles.body:
Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff is projected to have won re-election in Georgia, defeating Republican challenger Mike Collins and pushing the crucial swing state deeper into Democratic control.

Ossoff, a rising star in the Democratic Party, portrayed his opponent as loyal to a "failed president" and made the rising cost of living a central issue in the campaign. Georgia voted for Donald Trump in 2024.

Collins had blamed rising cost of living on former President Joe Biden and defended his support for Trump's war in Iran.

With polls suggesting Ossoff held a solid lead in the race, Republicans had diverted resources from Georgia to other contests.

News of Ossoff's projected victory, which was announced less than an hour after polls closed, rippled through the Georgia Democrats watch party in Atlanta with supporters cheering and clapping.

He began his remarks by thanking his family and voters in Georgia for their support, replying "I love you, too", in response to shouts coming from the jubilant crowd.

He returned to many of the points he made on the campaign trail, expressing his concern about the economic woes faced by everyday Americans, while attacking big pharma and corporate America and alleged corruption in the White House.

"This moment is an opening not for restoration, but for reformation," Ossoff said. "And so, amidst our celebration tonight, we must acknowledge that the underlying crisis gripping our Republic remains, and that therefore, our most vital work lies ahead."

The race was one of the first major contests projected as part of the midterms on Tuesday, which will shape the rest of Donald Trump's presidency. The outcome will determines which party - Trump's Republicans or opposition Democrats - controls Congress.

Brian Kemp, Georgia's term-limited Republican governor, was the favoured candidate to run against Ossoff, but he declined.

Political pundits suspected that Kemp had avoided running, wary of Ossoff's rising star power, with rumours swirling that the Democrat could be mulling a run for president in 2028.

Throughout his campaign, Ossoff downplayed such rumours, saying on multiple occasions that he has "zero interest" in a presidential bid.

His messaging on the campaign trail focused on the economy and voter concerns around affordability, which exit polls show was the top issue for many.

He often hammered Collins, who is currently serving in the US House of Representatives, for voting to support Trump's tariffs which have been linked to rising inflation.

His victory was not unexpected but Republicans had still hoped this would be a more competitive race. It's a state that had previously voted reliably red for decades. President Donald Trump won it in 2024, after Joe Biden eked out a narrow win there in 2020.

An easy win by Ossoff in Georgia could portend a good night for Democrats, though it's still too early to know.

The win could also ramp up speculation about his 2028 plans. The Georgia Democrat is considered a potential leading contender if he throws his hat in the ring.

articles.title: Jon Ossoff wins Georgia Senate race, defeating Republican Mike Collins
articles.summary: Ossoff is re-elected to a second term, winning a key seat for Democrats as the party tries to retake the Senate.
articles.body:
Incumbent Democratic US Senator Jon Ossoff has won re-election in the state of Georgia, one of the midterm cycle’s marquee contests.

He has defeated Republican Congressman Mike Collins, a staunch ally of President Donald Trump who faced intense scrutiny during the campaign regarding alleged ties to people espousing white supremacist ideology.

Ossoff, who has served as a US senator since 2021, campaigned on affordability, healthcare, and government accountability.

Collins, meanwhile, focused on the president’s agenda, immigration enforcement and reducing the size of the government.

Republicans had hoped to defeat Ossoff, the first Jewish senator in a state that backed former President Joe Biden in 2020 before reversing course and narrowly supporting Trump four years later.

Ossoff, seen by some as a possible contender for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination, will rejoin his fellow Democrat in the Senate, Raphael Warnock, Georgia’s first Black senator, who is also rumoured to be considering a run for the presidency.

Georgia’s US Senate seats were critical for building the Democratic Party’s power in Congress and in the South, a largely Republican stronghold.

Ossoff was leading Collins 63 percent to 29 percent with 56 percent of votes counted, according to the Associated Press news agency.

Trump won Georgia narrowly in 2024 after losing the state to Biden in the 2020 presidential election.

In 2023, Trump and others were charged in Georgia with attempting to overturn the 2020 election loss by pressuring a senior state official to recalculate the results in his favour. The case was dismissed after Trump returned to office in 2025.

After the results were called, Ossoff said American voters have rejected “lame duck” President Trump by handing the Democratic candidates “sweeping and decisive victories”.

“In sweeping and decisive victories the American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption and incompetence of the failed lame duck President Donald J Trump,” Ossoff said after defeating Republican Mike Collins for Georgia’s US Senate seat.

“The fact is we’ve been too long mired in small and selfish politics bought by big money, unmoored from fixed, moral principles, and resigned to intractable division,” the senator from Georgia added.

articles.title: Democratic Gov. Wes Moore wins re-election in deep-blue Maryland
articles.summary: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, a potential 2028 Democratic presidential contender, sailed to a re-election victory on Tuesday, NBC News projects.
articles.body: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, a potential 2028 Democratic presidential contender, sailed to a re-election victory on Tuesday, NBC News projects. Moore, who defeated former Republican state lawmaker Dan Cox in a rematch of the 2022 race, made history four years ago when he became Maryland’s first Black governor. During his first term, Moore at times clashed with his fellow Democrats, most notably over redistricting, when state legislative leaders rejected the governor’s calls to redraw congressional districts to eliminate the state’s lone Republican-held seat. At the polls on Tuesday, Maryland voters got the chance to weigh in on a proposed constitutional amendment that would allow state lawmakers to redraw congressional districts in a way that benefits Democrats. The governor also stepped into the national spotlight in the middle of his first term after a bridge collapse in Baltimore in early 2024 killed six people and shut down an international port. On the campaign trail, Cox pitched himself as the better option to manage the rebuilding of the bridge, telling voters that he could get the project done on a faster timeline than Moore. The rebuilding has faced several delays, including after Maryland parted ways this year with the Nebraska-based contractor Kiewit Infrastructure over a budget dispute. Moore’s travel to battleground states like Michigan, Nevada and Georgia to campaign alongside Democratic gubernatorial candidates this year fueled speculation that he may run for the White House. Moore demurred at a gubernatorial debate in October when asked whether he would commit to serving a full four-year term if re-elected. “I would not be running for re-election if I was not committed to the people of Maryland,” he told a panel of local political reporters. Asked last year on NBC News’ “Meet the Press” whether he was considering a 2028 presidential campaign, Moore said, “I’m not running for president.” Several other Democratic governors who are seen as possible presidential candidates, including Pennsylvania’s Josh Shapiro and Illinois’ JB Pritzker, were also on the ballot Tuesday. On the campaign trail in Maryland, Moore touted his work reducing violent crime rates in Baltimore, raising the statewide minimum wage and reducing teacher vacancy rates throughout Maryland. He also highlighted the times he’s sparred with President Donald Trump, including over the president’s deportation agenda and the tariffs he imposed on foreign goods. The governor also responded to allegations from conservative media outlets earlier this year that he had mischaracterized his military record in a book, blaming certain inaccuracies on the effects grief and stress can have on memory. During his first campaign, in 2022, Moore also faced allegations that he had misrepresented his upbringing in his memoir “The Other Wes Moore.”

articles.title: Democrats hold firm in Georgia as Republicans fail to flip prized Senate seat
articles.summary: Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff defeated Rep. Mike Collins in Georgia's 2026 midterms Senate race after clashes over immigration and Trump's tariffs.
articles.body: The Fox News Decision Desk projects that Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia has defeated Republican challenger Rep. Mike Collins. Ossoff, once considered by the GOP to be the most vulnerable Democratic senator seeking re-election in the 2026 midterms, will now keep his job representing the southeastern battleground state in the U.S. Senate. He took an early lead in the race when polls closed Tuesday night, which only expanded as the hours wore on. 2026 MIDTERM ELECTION DAY RESULTS: LIVE UPDATES His victory means Georgia, a one-time red bastion that swung to the center in recent years, will continue to have two Democrats representing the state in the Senate. He's the second Democratic senator to hold his seat on Tuesday night after Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., was also projected to win re-election. "A workhorse for the people of Georgia, Senator Ossoff has spent the last six years in the U.S. Senate providing outstanding constituent services, standing up for children, and fighting to make life better," the Senate Democrats' campaign arm said in a statement after Ossoff's victory. "Georgians sent him back to the Senate because they know he will always show up for them, and now he’ll continue putting Georgia families first." Ossoff and fellow Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock were both elected in runoff elections at the end of the 2020 cycle, ending a decade and a half of Georgia's all-Republican representation in the Senate. Weeks earlier, former President Joe Biden became the first Democrat to carry the state in nearly three decades. DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB But Georgia shifted back to the right in 2024, with President Donald Trump reclaiming the state and winning the White House. At the start of the 2026 cycle, Georgia was atop the GOP's target list of seats to flip, and Republicans aimed to hold their 53-47 Senate majority. While Ossoff built a massive campaign war chest as he cruised unopposed to renomination, Collins was part of a combustible three-way GOP primary Senate battle with Rep. Buddy Carter and former college football coach Derek Dooley, who was supported by popular term-limited conservative Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp. Collins and Dooley advanced to a June runoff, which Collins won due in part to an eleventh-hour Trump endorsement. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER In the general election showdown, Collins made illegal immigration a centerpiece of his campaign, spotlighting the Laken Riley Act, which he authored. The law requires the detention of certain illegal immigrants who are arrested for, charged with, convicted of or admit to committing specified offenses. Ossoff voted for the measure but has criticized the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement tactics. Collins also accused Ossoff of supporting policies that drove up inflation and taxes, while the senator targeted Collins over his backing of Trump's tariffs and the war in Iran, which triggered a surge in gas and diesel prices and an overall rise in the cost of living. During their debates, Ossoff also put Collins on defense over a House ethics investigation into whether the congressman abused taxpayer funds by hiring the girlfriend of his former chief of staff for work she allegedly did not perform. Collins has insisted the issue is simply a "complaint" with no merit. Collins also faced heat over social media posts by his son-in-law — a social media influencer on the far right — that shared Nazi imagery and antisemitic conspiracy theories. Ossoff, meanwhile, faced questions about receiving campaign funds from Reid Hoffman, a venture capitalist whose name appeared in the Epstein files. While GOP-aligned outside groups initially spent big bucks to back Collins and make up for his massive fundraising deficit in his battle against Ossoff, the Republican spigot was cut back substantially in the final weeks leading up to Election Day. The move was a sign that many Republicans were giving up on their hopes of flipping the Senate seat in Georgia. Ossoff, whom pundits view as a potential 2028 Democratic presidential contender, has repeatedly said he has "zero interest" in running for the White House next cycle. And in a debate with Collins last month, he pledged to serve out his full six-year Senate term if re-elected. Hank Johnson before working as managing director of an investigative documentary production company. He first grabbed national attention in 2017, when he narrowly lost a special congressional election for a House seat that had long been a GOP stronghold. Collins, who is also a Georgia native, is the son of the late Rep. Mac Collins. A businessman and the co-founder along with his wife of a trucking company, he was first elected to Congress in 2022.

articles.title: Former Gov. Roy Cooper wins North Carolina’s Senate race, flipping the seat for Democrats
articles.summary: Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper has defeated former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley in the contest for North Carolina’s open Senate seat, NBC News projects.
articles.body: Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper has defeated former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley in the contest for North Carolina’s open Senate seat, NBC News projects. Cooper’s victory secures a crucial flip for Democrats as they try to take control of the Senate. The party must gain a net of four seats to clinch a majority. The result also marks the first time a Democrat has won a Senate seat in North Carolina since 2008. Cooper will succeed retiring GOP Sen. Thom Tillis, who grew increasingly critical of President Donald Trump during his second term and chose not to seek re-election. The race was initially expected to be one of the most hotly contested across the Senate landscape. But in the closing weeks of the campaign, a top Republican super PAC canceled its ad spending in the race to focus more on protecting seats in more conservative territory as Cooper built a solid lead in the polls. Follow live updates on the midterm elections The abandonment of North Carolina as a front-line battleground resulted from several factors. First, Cooper, a popular former two-term governor, enjoyed high name recognition, while Republicans had few attacks to lob his way. A prized recruit for national Democrats, Cooper also avoided a contentious primary and focused his campaign almost entirely on the cost of living, a top voter concern. Whatley, who had previously led the state party and earned national recognition as RNC chairman during the 2024 election, had not run for elected office before. Trump, who urged him to launch a bid for the seat, and Vice President JD Vance rallied on several occasions with Whatley down the final stretch to give him a boost. But even Trump signaled in the closing weeks that Cooper was likely to win. “He’s going to become your senator,” Trump said at an October rally in the state. “And it’s crazy.” As voters soured on the economy and the Iran war, Whatley could not escape or distance himself from an increasingly unpopular president in the key battleground state. It was also the first midterm Senate race to take place in North Carolina with Trump in power, an environment that would be tougher for Republicans given traditional backlashes to the party that controls the White House. The state did not hold a Senate contest in 2018, Trump’s last midterm.

articles.title: GOP Sen. Ashley Moody wins special Senate election for Marco Rubio’s old seat in Florida
articles.summary: Moody, a former state attorney general who was appointed to succeed Rubio, defeated Democrat Angie Nixon, NBC News projects.
articles.body: Sen. Ashley Moody. R-Fla., defeated Democrat Angie Nixon in the special election for Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s old Senate seat, NBC News projects. Moody was considered the overwhelming favorite headed into the general election against Nixon, a Democratic Socialists of America-aligned candidate who scored an upset victory in the Democratic primary but faced a cash disadvantage throughout the general election. Though Moody secured victory, Nixon’s surprise primary night win did elevate the race nationally as her emergence piqued the interest of progressives across the country. Democrats saw her candidacy as an opportunity to gain a footing in a state where their party has not won a Senate race since 2012. Follow live updates on the midterm elections Ultimately, Moody continued the GOP’s run of dominance after she largely ran a careful, traditional Florida Republican campaign. She will serve the final two years of the term Rubio won in 2022; the seat will be on the ballot again in 2028 for a full term. Moody relied on her significant fundraising advantage to flood the airwaves in a state of 23 million people, where being able to afford the pricey ad rates is seen as key to victory. Moody did face some criticism for declining to debate and doing fewer public events than Nixon, who blanketed the state with in-person events and became a regular on both traditional state media and the center-left podcast circuit. “Ashley Moody should take a page out of Angie Nixon’s book,” Florida Democratic Party Chair Nikki Fried said at a news conference last month in Tallahassee. “Stop hiding behind attacks. Show up and talk to the people you work for, because Ashley Moody is asking Floridians for their vote, and if she won’t answer their questions, they’ll give her their answer in November.” The event included a sign that read “Where is Ashley Moody?” Those hits, however, were not enough to pull down Moody, who also faced criticism for her ties to the Hope Florida scandal, which involved $10 million for a Medicaid settlement being directed to a charity tied to Florida first lady Casey DeSantis. A political committee ultimately used that money to oppose a 2024 ballot measure that would have legalized recreational marijuana in the state. Moody, who was the state attorney general at the time, had to sign off on the deal. She has denied any wrongdoing, and no charges were brought after a state prosecutor impaneled a grand jury to review the matter. Moody’s main line of attack was focused on Nixon’s being too liberal for a state that now has 1.5 million more registered Republicans than Democrats, a massive recent reversal after Democrats held an advantage for decades. Much of Moody’s messaging and campaign ads focused on policies proposed by the Democratic Socialists of America more broadly, even as Nixon publicly distanced herself from them. “Angie Nixon is actually a socialist,” a narrator says in one of the spots that focused on Democratic Socialists of America issues like “abolishing the police,” which Nixon said she does not want to do. Moody had won two statewide elections for attorney general, but it was her first time on the ballot for the Senate. Gov. Ron DeSantis appointed her to the seat after Rubio was tapped to serve in Trump’s Cabinet.

articles.title: Democrat Roy Cooper flips North Carolina US Senate seat
articles.summary: Roy Cooper beat out Republican Michael Whatley.
articles.body:
Democrat Roy Cooper has won North Carolina’s United States Senate race, marking a significant pickup for the party as it looks to take back control of the chamber.

Cooper, a moderate former two-term governor, is the first Democrat to be elected to one of the state’s two US Senate seats since 2008, when former President Barack Obama carried it in his first White House bid.

He replaces outgoing Republican Senator Thom Tillis, who opted not to seek a third term in office after becoming a frequent critic of US President Donald Trump.

Since becoming the Democrats’ Senate nominee, Cooper consistently led his Republican opponent, former Republican National Committee chairman Michael Whatley, forcing Republicans to pull funding for Whatley’s campaign.

Cooper’s win is significant in a state that has narrowly voted for Trump three times since 2016.

Cooper said in his victory speech that he wants to combat “chaos and corruption in Washington” and pledged to work towards ending the US war against Iran after winning the US Senate election in North Carolina.

“Chaos and corruption in Washington were hurting our people. Today, you said, ‘This has to stop.’ And, as your new United States senator, I am ready to take that message to Washington,” Cooper said.

“We have to work to make healthcare, housing, and groceries more affordable, to end this war and stop the pain at the pump,” the former North Carolina governor added.

articles.title: Tuesday’s elections bring historic first for Black governors
articles.summary: Wins by Byron Donalds in Florida, Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia and Wes Moore in Maryland mean multiple Black governors will serve simultaneously for the first time.
articles.body: For the first time in U.S. history, multiple elected Black governors will serve at the same time — and it remains possible that voters will elect more this year than the four who have already won. That historic first is the result of Democratic Gov. Wes Moore’s winning re-election in Maryland, Republican Rep. Byron Donalds’ prevailing in the Florida governor’s race and Georgia Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms’ winning in her state. Hours later, David Crowley won the race for governor in Wisconsin, making him the fourth Black governor to have won Tuesday night. Before those wins, the only elected Black governors in U.S. history had been Moore; Deval Patrick, a Democrat who was elected Massachusetts’ governor in 2006; and Doug Wilder, a Democrat who was elected Virginia’s governor in 1989. None served simultaneously. In an interview with NBC News last month, Donalds said the history-making aspect of his candidacy was “very special.” “From a larger perspective, there’s so much that has been talked about in politics over the last couple decades around race. Obviously, the country has had some real negative parts of our history surrounding race,” he said. “I’m humbled to be in this position, but I think it says a lot more about the state [of Florida] than it does about me.” Bottoms, Donalds, Moore and Crowley may not stay in such rare company for long: Four other Black major-party candidates for governor are on the ballot Tuesday. That includes state Attorney General Aaron Ford in Nevada, where he is running against incumbent Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo. In South Carolina, another Black Democrat, state Rep. Jermaine Johnson, faces a more difficult path to victory in the traditionally red state’s race for governor. On the Republican side, Rep. John James is running in a competitive governor’s race against Democrat Jocelyn Benson, while Minnesota state House Speaker Lisa Demuth is seen as an underdog in Minnesota’s gubernatorial contest.

articles.body: Paul Pelosi is banned from getting behind the wheel for six months after crashing into a parked car and fleeing in California wine country, landing the former House speaker’s husband back in court four years after his DUI conviction. Pelosi, 86, struck an unoccupied parked vehicle in Yountville July 3 and fled, Napa County District Attorney Allison Haley said Tuesday. The husband of former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., pleaded no contest to misdemeanor hit-and-run and a traffic infraction for making an unlawful turn. PAUL PELOSI ABSENT FROM FIRST COURT APPEARANCE ON HIT-AND-RUN CHARGE IN NAPA COUNTY CRASH CASE Napa County Superior Court Judge Scott R.L. Young placed Pelosi on probation for one year and prohibited him from driving for six months, the maximum period allowed under the California Vehicle Code provisions cited by prosecutors. PELOSI STAFFER PUMPS THE BRAKES WHEN PRESSED ON HUSBAND'S HIT-AND-RUN: 'THAT'S ENOUGH' Deputies later located Pelosi about a half-mile away. TIGER WOODS SET FOR PLEA CHANGE HEARING AFTER DUI ARREST FOLLOWING FLORIDA ROLLOVER CRASH That conviction required him to attend a DUI education program and use an ignition interlock device. He was also sentenced to and ordered to pay restitution and fines. His driving history also includes a 1957 crash in San Mateo County that killed his 19-year-old brother, The New York Times reported. Pelosi was behind the wheel, but a jury cleared him of wrongdoing. More recently, Pelosi accumulated traffic infractions across four Bay Area counties, according to the Times. The outlet reported violations in Napa, San Mateo, Marin and San Francisco involving speeding, running a red light, driving against traffic on a one-way street and cellphone use without a hands-free device. articles.title: Democrat Annie Andrews defeats GOP Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina, a major upset
articles.summary: NBC News projects that Graham failed to secure a full term after she was appointed to the seat held by her late brother.
articles.body: Democrats notched an upset victory in South Carolina’s Senate race, NBC News projects, with Annie Andrews toppling Republican Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed this year to succeed her late brother, longtime Sen. Lindsey Graham. Andrews, a pediatrician, will be the state’s first Democratic senator in more than 20 years. President Donald Trump carried South Carolina by more than 17 percentage points two years ago. Gov. Henry McMaster appointed Darline Graham, a former administrator in state government, in July after Lindsey Graham, a five-term senator and stalwart fixture of Washington, died suddenly because of a heart problem. Follow live updates on the midterm elections Darline Graham then decided to run for a full term, starting in a special primary election, but she soon drew criticism for lacking fluency on some policy issues. She admitted in a debate with a Republican rival that she was “not that informed on national security,” though she went on to win the GOP nomination. Although the race was seen as a long shot for Democrats, Graham’s weaknesses prompted the Cook Political Report to shift it in September from “solidly” Republican to “likely” Republican. Meanwhile, Andrews significantly outraised and outspent Graham, who had to start her campaign from scratch mid-election cycle. In the final pre-election fundraising period, Andrews’ campaign raised more than $4 million, mostly from online donors, and spent over $4.6 million in two weeks. Graham’s campaign raised about $90,000 and spent $65,000. The race attracted a surge in outside spending in the closing stretch. The Senate Leadership Fund, a GOP super PAC, spent $13 million to boost Graham, while the Senate Majority PAC, which is aligned with Democratic leadership, announced a last-minute $750,000 digital buy. Andrews and Graham traded barbs in a debate last month, with Graham accusing Andrews of being unwilling to “stand up to socialist Democrats,” while Andrews said Graham was little more than a rubber stamp for Trump’s agenda. Andrews said she supported the Second Amendment — but Graham noted that Andrews has been a senior adviser to Everytown, the prominent gun control advocacy group. Andrews has also been accused of backpedaling on previous language signaling emphatic support for transgender people. Graham said Andrews has been “deceiving the people of South Carolina” and has “flip-flopped on everything.” Graham also made a notable break from Trump last month after he announced he would waive sanctions against Russia, going around a new law that was named for her brother. “Personally, I would choose to put the pressure on Russia to end the war and get gas prices down,” Graham told reporters at a campaign event. “Because I don’t trust Putin, and I don’t trust Russia.” Her remarks came even as Trump was scheduled to appear at a campaign stop for her in the state.
