articles.body:
Democrats won control of the House of Representatives with what could be their largest majority in nearly two decades, NBC News projects, as voters delivered a stunning rebuke to President Donald Trump and Republicans.

The House projection is based on an analysis that Democrats will win about 255 House seats — an estimate that could still tick up or down by a few seats but will be well beyond the 218 needed to secure a majority.

NBC News has projected the Democrats will also flip control of the Senate, putting them in charge of both chambers.

Democrats needed to win a net of just three seats to take back the majority. The blue wave washed over many more GOP-held seats than that — from the East Coast to Texas' Rio Grande Valley — most in districts that Trump carried in 2024.

A quartet of GOP incumbents in Pennsylvania were defeated. Democrat Bob Harvie beat GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, a leader of the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus; Democrat Bob Brooks knocked off GOP Rep. Ryan Mackenzie in the 7th Congressional District; Paige Cognetti bested GOP Rep. Rob Bresnahan in the 8th District; and Democrat Janelle Stelson ousted GOP Rep. Scott Perry, a former chairman of the far-right Freedom Caucus, in the 10th District.

In Virginia, Democratic former Rep. Elaine Luria won back her old seat, defeating Republican Rep. Jen Kiggans in the Virginia Beach area, while Democrat Shannon Taylor upset longtime GOP Rep. Rob Wittman outside Richmond.

Another big name in Republican politics, Rep. Tom Kean Jr. of New Jersey, lost his race for re-election to Democrat Rebecca Bennett. Rep. Victoria Spartz, R-Ind., the first Ukrainian-born member of Congress, who frequently clashed with Trump and GOP leaders, also was defeated. And in Colorado, Democratic state Rep. Manny Rutinel trounced GOP Rep. Gabe Evans.

One of the biggest prizes of the night for Democrats was Richard Ojeda II's upset of Rep. Richard Hudson, R-N.C. As chairman of the House GOP's campaign arm, Hudson was responsible for protecting GOP incumbents and the majority.

The Democrats' victory was widely seen as a referendum on Trump's unpopular policies, including his tough immigration crackdown, the eight-month Iran war and tariffs on U.S. allies that drove up the prices of gas, groceries and other goods.

When the party takes control of the chamber on Jan. 3, it will be the first time in Trump's second term that he won't have full control of Congress.

Since he returned to the White House, Trump has tested the limits of his executive powers, dismantling federal agencies through the Department of Government Efficiency , unilaterally imposing sweeping tariffs and rescinding congressionally approved funding — all while the GOP-controlled House and Senate mostly looked the other way.

The House Democratic leader, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who barnstormed across the country in the final weeks of the campaign, is expected to make history on Jan. 3 when he is sworn in as the first Black speaker of the House.

He walked into his election night watch party to raucous cheers as the rap song "Unbelievable," by the Notorious B.I.G., played on the speakers. The midterm results show the "American people are crying out for transformational change," Jeffries told supporters.

"Today begins the great American comeback. The American people have spoken all across the land, in the North, in the South, in the East, in the West, in the Midwest, from sea to shining sea. The American people have spoken and made clear they've had enough of the extremism, enough of the corruption," Jeffries said at the gathering in Washington.

"They want a Congress that's going to deliver for the American people," he said, "and that is exactly what House Democrats will do as soon as we get into office in January."

With their new majority, Democrats will take control of House committees, gaining subpoena power and the ability to conduct oversight investigations of Trump's administration, family and business ventures. That could take up considerable time and resources for Trump and his allies, forcing uncomfortable public hearings or prompting legal showdowns over subpoenas.

And in a callback to Trump's first term, some Democrats have vowed to impeach him for a third time, though there is an internal debate about whether that's the right political path.

Jeffries told NBC News' " Meet the Press " that Democrats "haven't ruled anything in and we haven't ruled anything out" on impeachment.

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., now poised to become chairman of the powerful Oversight Committee in January, said his panel plans to focus on "Trump family corruption," including Trump's cryptocurrency ventures , which have earned him more than $1 billion. The panel will also scrutinize "abuses" by ICE and the Department of Homeland Security, corporate corruption and the Jeffrey Epstein files.

Aside from investigative power, House Democrats will also command the ability to pass legislation with a simple majority. Jeffries has said Democrats would focus on four areas : reversing Trump's cuts to Medicaid, extending the Affordable Care Act credits, restoring congressional authority related to tariffs and stopping Trump's war with Iran.

"I wouldn't characterize it as investigating them like crazy. We're going to follow the facts, apply the law, be guided by the Constitution and let the chips fall where they may," Jeffries told reporters at Democrats' campaign headquarters before the election.

The results are a blow to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who was launched from obscurity into the top job and has led House Republicans for the past three years. It's unclear whether Johnson, a close Trump ally, will fight to remain as minority leader or step aside; the latter would trigger a fiercely competitive GOP race to replace him.

House Democrats had the political wind at their backs; they needed to flip a net of just three seats to win back the majority they lost in 2022. And Trump's dismal approval rating was a major factor in the GOP's loss.

Historically, the president's party tends to lose seats in midterm elections. Only in two midterms in the modern era did a party buck that trend — in 1998, when voters punished Republicans for impeaching President Bill Clinton, and in 2002, as President George W. Bush rallied support in the wake of the 9/11 terrorist attacks.

Still, the battle for House control played out primarily on GOP turf this cycle, with Democrats already holding 215 seats, including a dozen in battleground districts. On top of that, results of this cycle's mid-decade redistricting wars ended up favoring Republicans slightly, though Democrats quickly moved to neutralize what could have been a large GOP advantage.

Trump fired the first shot in the summer of 2025, when he urged GOP allies in Texas to redraw their congressional lines to help the party pick up as many as five seats. Republicans also redrew maps in places like Florida, North Carolina, Tennessee, Alabama, Louisiana and Missouri in a bid to win more seats.

But Democrats countered in California, with Gov. Gavin Newsom, former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and their allies successfully rallying support for Proposition 50 , which approved a new congressional map drawn by state Democrats. That map helped Democrats pick up GOP-held seats.

While the GOP successfully picked up a handful of majority-Black, Democratic-held seats in the South, the Supreme Court blocked Missouri Republicans' new congressional map, essentially preserving the Kansas City seat of longtime Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver.

"We made a promise to aggressively push back against the MAGA extremist effort to rip the election away from the American people by gerrymandering the possibility of Democrats winning the majority out of existence," Jeffries said before the election, adding that the redistricting wars will continue in the 120th Congress.

"This fight is not over; we've just gotten started," he added. "It will continue into the next Congress until we pass legislation signed into law by a future president that will prohibit mid-decade gerrymandering from ever happening again."

articles.title: Mamdani-backed socialist wins NYC House seat as DSA expands its reach in Congress
articles.summary: Claire Valdez's DSA-backed win in NY-7 deepens a growing rift dividing New York Democrats, with Hakeem Jeffries and John Fetterman weighing in.
articles.body: Claire Valdez, a Democratic candidate for Congress in New York’s 7th Congressional District, was the projected winner in her congressional race against Republican challenger Melvin Rivera, a community activist, on Tuesday evening in the race to fill the seat of outgoing Rep. Nydia Velázquez, D-N.Y. Velázquez, who has held the seat since 2013 and has been a member of Congress since 1993, is retiring. The district’s strong Democratic lean made Valdez the favorite, and her victory marks another noteworthy win for the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) in the 2026 midterms. MAMDANI-BACKED SOCIALISTS LOOK TO TAKE NEW YORK PLAYBOOK NATIONWIDE AFTER PRIMARY VICTORIES In the June primary, New York’s 7th District was seen as a proxy for the direction of the party. During that race, Valdez faced off against a crowded field of other congressional hopefuls. Among them was Antonio Reynoso, the Brooklyn borough president. While Valdez enjoyed the backing of the DSA and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a self-proclaimed socialist, Reynoso received support from more established Democrats, including Velázquez. "It’s very nice to get to New York for a few years and to have opinions about other elected officials without knowing the history and the struggle and who was there fighting corrupt government," Velázquez told The New York Times ahead of the primary. JEFFRIES' SOCIALISM DILEMMA: NEW YORK VICTORIES EXPOSE DEMOCRATIC PARTY DIVIDE "Now, all of the sudden, people want to come in and decide who is the best candidate with total disregard to the history, the background." U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries didn’t endorse in the race but acknowledged the divide at play in the race, noting the DSA’s break with many other New York Democratic figures, including Letitia James, the state’s attorney general. "Nydia Velázquez and a coalition of very progressive Democrats, including Tish James … along with the Working Families Party and many of the unions … are on one side of that race, with DSA on the other," Jeffries told reporters in June. Valdez based her primary platform on promises to abolish ICE and implement a Green New Deal-style approach to climate change. She also supports universal rent control and Medicare for All. Her platform attracted the backing of the DSA in January. DEMOCRATIC CONGRESSMAN WARNS OF 'DANGEROUS' SOCIALIST AGENDA AFTER FAR-LEFT PRIMARY WINS "With this endorsement, Valdez’s campaign will be powered by the same volunteer army that propelled Mayor Zohran Mamdani to victory in 2025… Valdez is the only candidate running in NY-7 who has committed to not taking money from the real estate industry," the group stated in a press release. Democratic strategist Mally Smith told Fox News Digital, "It is not surprising she won given how blue that district is." "We are a big tent party and that means there are going to be some folks on the far left who win. But for us to win in competitive red or swing states we should nominate candidates like Roy Cooper and James Talarico," Smith added. Valdez isn’t the only DSA-backed candidate in New York to prompt considerations about the future of the Democratic Party. In a very similar primary race, Darializa Avila Chevalier, another DSA candidate, beat out incumbent Rep. Adriano Espaillat, D-N.Y., a high-ranking Democrat and the chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus. The wins have captured national attention and drawn criticism from some Democrats who have criticized the DSA’s growth in the party. Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., who has not shied away from confrontations, has been one of the few Democrats to express alarm about the kind of candidates carrying the party’s banner. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I mean, you look at some of the things that people have said. Abolish prison, abolish the border, abolish ICE, I mean these crazy people — I have colleagues in my caucus that refuse to even call this out," Fetterman told Fox News Digital earlier this year.

articles.title: Massive upset: Andrews downs Trump-backed Graham in ruby-red South Carolina
articles.summary: Annie Andrews, a pediatrician and political outsider, pulled off a historic upset in South Carolina's Senate race despite Trump's rally for Darlene Graham.
articles.body: The Fox News Decision Desk projects that Democratic challenger Annie Andrews has defeated appointed GOP Sen. Darline Graham, the younger sister of the late longtime Sen. Lindsey Graham, to win a six-year term representing South Carolina in the Senate. With her major upset, Andrews, a pediatrician who ran as an outsider, becomes the first Democrat in nearly three decades to win a Senate election in South Carolina. Having a very familiar name in South Carolina and receiving two 11th-hour campaign trail stops by President Donald Trump weren't enough to help push Graham over the finish line in the ruby-red southeastern state. DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB The race became increasingly competitive in the final weeks of the campaign. And outside groups aligned with Republicans and Democrats poured cash and resources into the ballot box showdown at the 11th hour. With some of the top nonpartisan political handicappers shifting the contest in the direction of the Democrats, Trump traveled to South Carolina with less than two weeks until Election Day to rally with Graham. "She’s smart and incredible. She’ll never let you down," Trump said as he praised Graham at an Oct. 21 stop in Upstate South Carolina. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Democratic strategist Mally Smith told Fox News Digital that "South Carolina bows to no king." "President Trump tried to hand-pick his successor in South Carolina, and the voters emphatically rejected his choice. Americans are sick of electing MAGA puppets to higher office who enable Trump’s erratic behavior and blatant corruption," said Smith. During the general election campaign, Graham emphasized her support for Trump’s agenda, continuing her brother’s work in the Senate, and spotlighting cost of living issues. "I know how it feels to live paycheck to paycheck. There's been many years in my life that I've lived paycheck to paycheck like a lot of South Carolinians. So I know they're feeling it at the gas pumps," Graham said in a recent interview on Fox News' "America Reports." "Suspending the gas tax, that's a temporary solution. I'm all for that. I'm glad that President Trump eased regulations on red-dyed diesel. I think that helps farmers. But the long-term solution is easing regulations on drilling and oil refineries." Andrews also made affordability, along with healthcare costs, a centerpiece of her Senate campaign, and highlighted her experience as a pediatrician working with children and families. "I never in a million years thought I would be running for federal office, let alone a US Senate seat, but I have 20 years of experience working inside America's broken healthcare system, coming face to face with all of Washington's failures in my hospital exam rooms. And I take that experience and I bring it to the campaign trail," Andrews emphasized in a recent Fox News Digital interview. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP After her brother's sudden death in July, GOP Gov. Henry McMaster appointed Graham to fill the remainder of the late senator's current term, which concludes at the end of this year. At the time of his death, Lindsey Graham had won renomination in South Carolina's June primary. With Trump's urging and support, Graham ran in a special Republican Senate nomination primary to succeed her brother. She defeated Rep. Ralph Norman in a late August runoff election after the two advanced two weeks earlier from a crowded 10-candidate primary.

articles.title: Trump Bedminster golf course falls to Dems as Republicans lose key House seat
articles.summary: Rebecca Bennett is projected to beat New Jersey's 7th Congressional District after defeating Tom Kean Jr., whose battle with depression kept him from Congress.
articles.body: A key New Jersey swing district is falling out of Republicans' grasp on Tuesday night in a critical victory for House Democrats. New Jersey's 7th Congressional District, which is where President Donald Trump's Bedminster golf course is located, is projected to be represented next year by former Navy helicopter pilot Rebecca Bennett after she was projected to defeat Rep. Tom Kean Jr., R-N.J. Kean, the son of former Garden State Gov. Tom Kean Sr., was seeking a third term representing the affluent area encompassing suburbs and exurbs of New York City. DEMS PICK CHALLENGER FOR GOP CONGRESSMAN WHO VANISHED FROM PUBLIC VIEW AMID HEALTH MYSTERY Multiple election forecasts, including Fox News Power Rankings, projected he would lose to Bennett in what was expected to be an overall difficult year for Republicans trying to keep their congressional majorities. Kean is known to keep a low profile on Capitol Hill. But he was thrust into the spotlight earlier this year over a four-month absence from Congress that he later revealed was due to his getting treatment for depression. He received some blowback, however, for not revealing the specifics of his issue until his return. REPUBLICAN CONGRESSMAN WILL END MONTHSLONG ABSENCE FROM DC AFTER MISSING 135 ROLL CALL VOTES "When I first informed the public that I was dealing with a medical issue, I was still trying to understand what was happening myself," Kean said on the House floor when he returned. "When I said I hoped to return in a matter of weeks, I believed it. Those were the best estimates the doctors could provide. But, as the over 48 million of my fellow Americans being treated for this illness have come to discover, there is no timeline for healing. There is no timeline for recovery. Only the work of getting better one day at a time." He defended Trump's economic record and war in Iran during his and Bennett's first and only debate, while she criticized the president's tariffs and blamed the Middle East conflict for the high gas prices Americans are grappling with. Kean told Fox News Digital of his own record in August. "I've been a really effective legislator who's brought things back to the district, who's listened to my constituents on their needs and their concerns, in contrast to my opponent, who has really been a very abject partisan," Kean said. Republicans across the U.S. have been sandbagged by Trump's low approval numbers despite the president crisscrossing the country in the weeks before the election in a bid to turn out the base. FOX NEWS POLL: AS ECONOMIC PAIN DEEPENS, DISAPPROVAL OF TRUMP HITS NEW HIGH Several House Republicans told Fox News Digital early Tuesday night that they had given up hope of keeping the majority. "It's a bloodbath," one senior House GOP aide said. And Kean's district was one of the earliest in which GOP groups waved the white flag. Fox News Digital was told by multiple sources last month that the House GOP leadeship-aligned Congressional Leadership Fund and Trump-aligned MAGA Inc. were pulling their investments out of the district to triage races in other parts of the country. A source close to Kean's campaign brushed it off at the time, telling Fox News Digital the campaign was set for cash. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., told attendees at a fundraiser for Kean that Fox News Digital attended in August, "We consider this a top three race, not just a top 10. That's how important it is to us. It has a target on its back."

articles.title: Hillary Clinton warns Dems may squander midterm victory if they fail to stay focused after election
articles.summary: Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton laid out a three-part Democratic agenda after the midterms covering affordability, anti-corruption and DOGE.
articles.body:
Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton warned on the "Pivot" podcast that even if Democrats score major victories in the midterms, they could squander their gains if they fail to focus on the issues that matter to voters most.

Clinton spoke with "Pivot" podcast co-hosts Kara Swisher and Scott Galloway at a live Election Night event and predicted a Democratic wave.

"I think we're going to wake up to a Democratic House and a Democratic Senate," she told the co-hosts.

Galloway agreed with Clinton's prediction but warned that it may be a short-term victory if Democrats do not respond to voter concerns.

"Let's count our chickens and assume we take the House and the Senate, and it's Nov. 4. I would argue it's a lease, not a mortgage; dating, not a relationship," Galloway said. "I think that it'll be a function of not them loving Democrats, but hating us less.

"What do you think the Democratic Party needs to do, or Democratic leadership, what are two or three things you think they need to do immediately such that we can turn this into something enduring going into '28 instead of just them flipping back in 24 months?"

Clinton agreed, warning that Democrats would need to capitalize on any midterm victories and follow through on their agenda if they want to win in 2028 as well.

"You're absolutely right, Scott. If the Democrats don't go in with an agenda and have the discipline to enact that agenda, then they're going to lose the kind of support that they're going to gain in this election," she said.

Clinton said Democrats could capitalize on potential midterm victories by focusing on affordability, corruption and investigations into the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).

"Number one, they ought to look at the affordability agenda . What's going to be in that? I think there are several things, one of which is healthcare costs," Clinton said.

"But there also can be even more fast-tracking of, you know, housing starts, taking a hard look at how we can, you know, shift the burden on fossil fuel costs from consumers to the oil and gas companies which have recorded record profits.

"So, I think that there's a lot of good work being done right now to put together an affordability package.

"Secondly, an anti-corruption package . You know, people have to feel that this issue of corruption is going to be front and center because it has been costing money," she said. "People have been benefiting at the expense of, you know, everyday Americans, consumers, people who get up every day and try to make a living."

The final step, she said, would be to do some investigations into DOGE's impact .

"We still don't even know the damage that Elon Musk did through DOGE," Clinton remarked. "We don't know what data was illegally taken, your social security data, your Medicare data … where is it? What's it being used for? We need to get to the bottom of this."

Hillary Clinton said Democrats should prioritize affordability, anti-corruption measures and investigations into DOGE's activities.

articles.title: Democrat James Talarico turns Texas Senate seat blue, defeating Ken Paxton
articles.summary: Talarico has made history in Texas, notching a Democratic Senate victory there for the first time since 1988, NBC News projects.
articles.body: Democrat James Talarico has pulled off an election win that was unthinkable for years, flipping a Senate seat in red Texas, NBC News projects — an against-the-odds victory that dislodged Republicans’ three-decade grip on the state, overcame a $168 million ad assault by the world’s wealthiest man and rebuked the MAGA movement in a state President Donald Trump won handily three times. Talarico, a state lawmaker and seminarian, defeated Trump-aligned state Attorney General Ken Paxton after he gained national prominence on a message centered on wealth disparity and corruption. All the while, he integrated Christian themes and sought to transcend traditional politics in a state where his party hadn’t won in years. He campaigned on a “top versus bottom instead of left versus right” message, telling supporters that the top 1% of wealthy Americans wanted the rest of the country to fight with one another instead of keep a check on those in power. Follow live updates on the midterm elections Meanwhile, on the Republican side, the “I told you so’s” were flying before voting even ended. Paxton has battled personal scandals for years, but Trump endorsed him over GOP Sen. John Cornyn in the primary anyway. In the general election, a line of prominent Republicans publicly pledged support for Talarico rather than back Paxton. The Republican-controlled state House impeached Paxton in 2023 before the state Senate acquitted him in a vote for which Trump took credit after he pressured the lawmakers. Paxton’s estranged wife, Angela Paxton, a state senator, publicly revealed that she had sought a divorce on “biblical grounds.” She ended up cutting an ad urging her party to support the ticket without ever mentioning Paxton. While Cornyn said he would back the Republican ticket, he never specifically endorsed Paxton, and he even held a joint fundraiser with former President George W. Bush for Republican Senate candidates that didn’t include him. Paxton still had plenty of firepower behind him, including nine figures’ worth of super PAC donations from Elon Musk. But it wasn’t enough. The end result: Democrats have grabbed control of a key Senate seat on Trump’s watch in a state that once epitomized the movement he built. Instead, it was Talarico who mobilized voters in the Lone Star State. Early voting numbers showed Texans showing up in record-breaking numbers in many counties, and Latino voters swung back toward Democrats after having supported Trump in the state in 2024. Early voting data showed that Hispanic voters had come out in massive numbers, including surges of young people and those who hadn’t cast ballots in 2022 or 2024. Talarico’s campaign caught fire early. When he launched his bid in Round Rock in 2025, he drew 1,500 people to a rally later that day. He went on to shatter fundraising records with the help of small-dollar donors from across the country. Talarico focused on appealing to independents and Republicans unhappy with Paxton’s history or with their party’s 30-year rule in the state. Two members of the legendary Bush family in Texas — Bush’s daughter Barbara and his brother Neil — threw their support behind Talarico. Talarico’s campaign early on made a strategic decision not to campaign with surrogates outside the state, trying to prevent Paxton from drawing parallels to national Democrats who might not play the same way in Texas. That meant there was no lift from the likes of former President Barack Obama, who rallied in states such as Michigan to stadium-sized crowds. Talarico had a knack for capturing the spotlight nonetheless. Podcaster Joe Rogan, who famously backed Trump in 2024, hosted Talarico on his show, urging him to run for president. Talarico’s invites from Stephen Colbert and Jimmy Kimmel drew the White House’s ire, leading to his being blocked from TV airtime, under a claim of a rarely enforced equal time rule. But that only meant interest exploded, generating millions of views and fundraising. Of the states up for grabs Tuesday, Texas is perhaps the biggest personal blow to Trump. His endorsement of Paxton in May, helping oust Cornyn, ripped open a chasm in the Republican Party that remained through Election Day. As Paxton struggled in polling and fundraising, Trump tried to mount a rescue mission. He visited Texas three times in October to hold rallies, hitting red areas along the way to boost turnout. Talarico steadily held a polling lead throughout the general election, though typically by the margin of error. It was a phenomenon unlike Beto O’Rourke, the last Democrat to come close to winning a statewide race in Texas, in 2018. Then, he narrowly lost his bid to oust Sen. Ted Cruz. In the closing days of the election, Talarico increasingly framed the race as a classic David-versus-Goliath tale — not between himself and Paxton, but between himself and Musk. He accused Musk — who has significant business interests in Texas — of trying to buy his own personal senator. Musk in recent days ratcheted up his attacks on Talarico on X, amplifying his past comments about transgender people and repeatedly calling him “weird.” Talarico campaigned heavily throughout the state, working to narrow margins in red parts of Texas that have overwhelmed other Democratic candidates in recent years. While Paxton did far fewer campaign events than Talarico over the summer, in October, Talarico disappeared from the trail as he recovered from the flu. Republicans opened an expensive ad campaign against Talarico over the airwaves, repeatedly airing ads that quoted him saying that God was “nonbinary” and that there were six sexes, as well as showing a video in which Talarico said he loved transgender children. Trump also amplified Talarico’s past comments in his Texas stump speeches. He often lauded Paxton as the “greatest attorney general in the country,” saying he stepped forward to combat Joe Biden’s presidency in ways that other attorneys general didn’t. Among the lawsuits Paxton filed on behalf of Texas: a complaint challenging the results of the 2020 presidential election. The U.S. Supreme Court threw it out. Even as Talarico cast Paxton as corrupt, he had this to say when he was asked in a recent interview whether he loved Paxton. “Yes, Ken Paxton is a child of God. He is my brother in Christ,” Talarico said. “It doesn’t mean there’s not accountability, right? Love requires accountability.”

articles.title: Trump country sees 20-year GOP grip on governor's mansion shattered
articles.summary: Democrat Amy Acton defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy in the Ohio governor race by cultivating a moderate image on affordability and education.
articles.body: The Fox News Decision Desk predicts Democrat Amy Acton will defeat Republican Vivek Ramaswamy in Ohio's closely watched gubernatorial race, delivering a major upset in a state that has not elected a Democratic governor in 20 years. Acton successfully ran a campaign appealing to voters across the aisle by presenting herself as the candidate who could address issues of affordability and public education. On the campaign trail, she painted Ramaswamy as out-of-touch, wealthy and pushing policies that benefited people like himself. During the election's closing weeks, Ramaswamy lost droves of support and faced bipartisan backlash over a campaign ad featuring Acton's estranged mother calling her daughter a liar who could not lead Ohio until she held herself accountable. The ad did not mention that Acton had been estranged from her mother since childhood or that her mother lost custody after Acton's stepfather was indicted on a charge of raping Acton when she was 12. RAMASWAMY OUTLINES KEY CONTRASTS WITH DEM OPPONENT LESS THAN 100 DAYS OUT FROM KEY GUBERNATORIAL ELECTION Still, Ramaswamy defended the ad amid the backlash, even as current Republican Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine called it "deeply troubling" and urged his campaign to take it down. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance defended Ramaswamy's decision to air it. The ad ultimately went off the air days before Election Day, with Ramaswamy's campaign saying its planned run had ended. Though Ramaswamy’s controversies took center stage in the national press, Acton’s record was not unblemished. Ramaswamy and his Republican allies honed in on Acton's record as director of the Ohio Department of Health, where she led the state's early response to the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. Conservatives pinned the state’s school and business closures, as well as a controversial decision to delay primary voting by closing polling stations, on Acton. This line of attack was complicated by DeWine. As criticism was being leveled against Acton, DeWine defended her by stating that "the buck stops with the governor," noting he had instructed her to go through with the voting delay. DeWine further complicated matters for the Ramaswamy campaign in April when he questioned whether the state could afford further tax cuts, casting doubt on a key plank of the Republican’s campaign pitch. The governor also criticized Ramaswamy’s proposal to close or consolidate Ohio’s public universities, while Democrats framed the plans as a way to pay for his proposed tax cuts by reducing access to education. DeWine did, however, officially endorse Ramaswamy over Acton. DAVID MARCUS: IN SPRINGFIELD, OHIO, ONLY TRUMP CAN MEND MAGA-CHAMBER OF COMMERCE RIFT Ramaswamy also faced criticism from both the left and right over awkward moments on the campaign trail, including a batting cage video that drew ridicule on social media. A controversial social media post Ramaswamy made on Christmas Day 2024, where he lambasted American culture as having "venerated mediocrity over excellence" while discussing foreign-born engineers, angered those on the right, including fellow Indian American Nikki Haley. Many right-wing commentators on X and other platforms still point to that post as a reason to distrust Ramaswamy. DAVID MARCUS: IN DAYTON, OHIO, BOTH PARTIES FACE BITTER POLITICAL DESPONDENCY Republicans sought throughout the campaign to tie Acton to unpopular pandemic-era restrictions she helped implement as Ohio's health director, while Acton sought to carve out a more moderate image on some issues. She broke with many in her party, for example, by opposing policies that allow biological males to compete in women's sports. Ramaswamy entered the race with deep ties to Trump's political movement. The former presidential candidate was initially tapped to help lead the Trump administration's Department of Government Efficiency alongside Elon Musk before leaving the effort as Trump took office to pursue his gubernatorial bid. He was also a prominent Trump surrogate after ending his own 2024 presidential campaign. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The last time Ohio elected a Democratic governor was in 2006, when Ted Strickland defeated Republican Ken Blackwell. Ramaswamy ran with no serious primary rivals and a significant financial advantage over Acton.

articles.title: California voters decide who will succeed Newsom in consequential governor's race
articles.summary: Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton battled over housing costs, homelessness and Trump in the race to succeed Gavin Newsom as governor.
articles.body: The Fox News Decision Desk projects former Biden Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Xavier Becerra will defeat Republican Steve Hilton in the race to succeed term-limited Gov. Gavin Newsom, keeping California's governorship in Democratic hands. Becerra has spent more than three decades in public office, beginning with his election to the California State Assembly in 1990 before serving over two decades in Congress. He left the House in 2017 after then-Gov. Jerry Brown appointed him California attorney general, won a full term in the post the following year and later served as President Joe Biden's HHS secretary from 2021 to 2025. Becerra and Hilton emerged from California's crowded nonpartisan top-two primary in June, when Becerra finished first with roughly 28% of the vote and Hilton advanced in second with about 25%. More than 9.4 million Californians cast ballots in the primary, according to certified results from the California secretary of state's office. CALIFORNIA FACES UNLIKELY TAX REVOLT AMID BILLIONS IN ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT HEALTHCARE COSTS Becerra's victory extends Democrats' long-running dominance of statewide politics in California, where registered Democrats substantially outnumber Republicans. A Republican has not won a California gubernatorial election since Arnold Schwarzenegger's re-election in 2006 and has not occupied the governor's mansion since he left office in January 2011. Hilton, a former Fox News host and onetime policy advisor to British Prime Minister David Cameron, campaigned as a change candidate, arguing that years of Democratic control in Sacramento had contributed to California's high cost of living, homelessness and other problems. He proposed cutting taxes and state spending, rolling back regulations and climate mandates and expanding energy production to lower housing, electricity and gasoline costs. Hilton also received President Donald Trump's endorsement but said during the general election that he would work with the administration while disagreeing with the president when necessary. Becerra will inherit a state confronting persistent challenges over housing and energy costs, homelessness and looming budget deficits. NEWSOM SPARS WITH TRUMP-APPOINTED PROSECUTOR OVER 20,000 SUSPECTED NONCITIZENS ON VOTER ROLLS Affordability was also a central theme of Becerra's campaign, with the Democrat arguing that rising costs threatened what he called the "California Dream." But he offered voters a markedly different prescription from Hilton, proposing a larger role for state programs and enforcement rather than broad cuts to taxes, spending and regulation. Becerra proposed accelerating housing construction, expanding childcare assistance and early education, strengthening Medi-Cal and cracking down on landlords he accused of price gouging. He also pointed to his record as HHS secretary, including efforts to lower prescription drug costs and expand access to health coverage. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER The candidates offered sharply different approaches to the Trump administration as well. Becerra campaigned on protecting California policies and programs from federal challenges, drawing on his record of repeatedly taking the first Trump administration to court during his tenure as state attorney general. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Becerra also reaffirmed during the campaign his support for protecting access to transgender medical procedures, including for transgender youth. He previously championed the issue as HHS secretary, when he defended leaving treatment decisions involving transgender minors to families and medical providers rather than politicians. Hilton previously told Fox News Digital that Californians are growing fed up with years of Democratic leadership, pointing to homelessness, high taxes and the soaring cost of living as reasons voters may be ready for a change. "I know everyone says, 'Well, it's California, Republicans can't win.' I don't know. I think people are sick of all this," Hilton said. "And they're sick of Becerra just taking them for granted, and I think we can win this election." Newsom was barred from seeking a third consecutive term after winning the governorship in 2018 and re-election in 2022. His departure comes amid continued speculation about a potential 2028 presidential bid. Becerra will be sworn in as California's 41st governor in January 2027.

articles.title: Democrat Rob Sand flips control of the Iowa governorship
articles.summary: NBC News projects that Sand, the state auditor, defeated Republican businessman Zach Lahn, making him the first Democrat to win the Iowa governor’s race in 20 years.
articles.body: State Auditor Rob Sand will be the next governor of Iowa, NBC News projects, making him the first Democrat to be elected to the office in 20 years. Sand, who ran as a moderate, defeated Republican businessman Zach Lahn to succeed retiring Republican Kim Reynolds in a state Donald Trump carried by 13 points in 2024. As the only Democratic statewide elected official in Iowa, Sand, 44, has long been seen as a rising star in a party that has sought to regain ground it lost in rural states in the Trump era. Sand cruised to the Democratic nomination this year, while Lahn, 40, pulled off an upset against Rep. Randy Feenstra in the Republican gubernatorial primary. In an expensive general election, Sand and his allies repeatedly cast Lahn as a carpetbagger and a “part-time Iowan” because he lived and voted in Kansas until recently and frequently traveled there during his campaign. Lahn explained in a debate why he was frequently in Kansas: “I have a blended family, and my kids split time,” he said. Lahn said Sand was “just like all the other Democrats” in TV ads and labeled him a “liberal billionaire” in a debate, pointing to Sand’s wife’s post as CEO of her family’s company. Lahn tried to tie Sand to the policy positions of out-of-state Democrats on immigration, energy and taxes and claimed that Sand’s wife’s company polluted Iowa’s waterways, which he rebutted. Pollution from agribusiness and Iowa’s rising cancer rates were central themes in Sand’s and Lahn’s campaigns. “I think there’s a lot of places of bipartisan agreement on this issue. It’s a really important one for a lot of people in Iowa,” Sand told NBC News in October. At a debate, Lahn told viewers, “For a very long time, we have seen the nitrate load in our water increase year after year,” adding that he would work toward “real solutions” if he were elected. Lahn won his GOP primary this year with support from members of the “Make America Healthy Again” movement that’s associated with Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. While Trump backed Feenstra in the primary, he endorsed Lahn afterward and appeared at rallies in the state in the lead-up to Election Day. As in other governor’s races across the country, Sand and Lahn sparred often about the economy and making life more affordable. Sand pledged to raise the minimum wage and impose policies to make healthcare and prescription drugs more affordable, while Lahn pledged to boost Iowa’s small businesses and cut taxes.

articles.title: Sherrod Brown, an Ohio Democrat, wins return to US Senate
articles.summary: More than $500m was spent on the contest, making it one of the most expensive Senate races in US history.
articles.body:
Democrat Sherrod Brown has mounted a successful return to the US Senate, handing a stinging defeat to Republicans who had hoped to hold on to the seat, according to Associated Press news agency projections.

Brown, who was ousted from the Senate two years ago, overcame a costly challenge by incumbent Republican Senator Jon Husted.

More than $500m was spent on advertising in the race, with US tech companies contributing tens of millions to defeat Brown. It was the second most expensive race of this midterm cycle and among the 10 costliest non-presidential races in US history, according to The Hill.

Husted, a strong ally of US President Donald Trump, was appointed to the seat in early 2025 to replace its previous holder, US Vice President JD Vance. He has supported a host of Trump’s second-term policies, including tax cuts, the Iran war and tariffs.

The Ohio race was seen as central in deciding which party controls the Senate. Both of the state’s seats are currently held by Republicans, one of whom helped secure the Senate for Republicans by beating Brown in 2024.

The cost of living was a major issue in the US Midwest, which is home to struggling former industrial cities and rural communities.

Brown championed his strong ties to labour unions and working-class communities in his bid to regain the seat. He will serve the remainder of Vance’s term, which runs until January 2029.

articles.title: Democrat Adam Hamilton pulls off upset over GOP Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas
articles.summary: NBC News projects that Hamilton, a pastor and former Republican, will become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in deep red Kansas since 1932.
articles.body: Adam Hamilton has defeated Republican Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas, NBC News projects, becoming the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the ruby red state since 1932. The upset victory in a state Donald Trump carried by 16 points in the 2024 election gives Democrats a major boost in the fight for the Senate majority. Hamilton, a minister at the largest Methodist congregation in the country, has never held public office and was registered as a Republican until earlier this year. Despite Kansas’ conservative history, it became a key battleground in the final stretch of the race. Amid growing backlash to Trump’s handling of the economy, Republican outside groups were forced to divert millions of dollars to boost Marshall. Democratic groups responded with their own ads, as well. Follow live updates on the midterm elections Running as a moderate, Hamilton, 62, garnered bipartisan support, including from GOP former Govs. Bill Graves and Mike Hayden. He had served on former President Barack Obama’s faith advisory council and preached at his 2013 inaugural prayer service. Hamilton and his allies hit Marshall, 66, on the high prices that resulted from the Iran war and Trump’s tariff agenda, as well as the healthcare cuts in the “big, beautiful bill” Republicans enacted last year. Rising diesel fuel and beef prices hit Kansas’ agricultural economy particularly hard. Democrats noted that Marshall repeatedly voted against resolutions to halt the conflict until Congress authorized it. They also pointed to comments in April when, responding to rising gas prices, Marshall said national security was “even more important than your pocketbook.” Still, Marshall did not distance himself from Trump to the degree that Republicans in other tough races did ahead of the election, though in September he demanded that federal immigration agents work with local law enforcement. Marshall, an obstetrician-gynecologist, also came under fire in September after The New York Times reported that he sued hundreds of patients over unpaid bills, resulting in dozens of arrest warrants for missed court dates. His lawyer said that while Marshall had set the interest rate of 18% on the bills, he had no involvement in warrants or arrests. Marshall dismissed the story as a “hit job.” Before he won his first term in the Senate by 11 points in 2020, Marshall served two terms in the House. While Kansas hasn’t had a Democratic senator in nearly 90 years, a Democrat, Laura Kelly, served the last two terms as governor.

articles.title: GOP governor defies Dem enthusiasm, tough political climate to win re-election in key swing state
articles.summary: Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte defeated Cinde Warmington to win a second term as New Hampshire governor despite a rough political climate for the GOP.
articles.body: The Fox News Decision Desk projects that Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte has defeated Democratic challenger Cinde Warmington in New Hampshire's gubernatorial election. Defying a rough political climate facing the GOP as well as Democratic Party enthusiasm, Ayotte won re-election to a second two-year term as the Northern New England swing state's governor. Ayotte, who also served two decades ago as state attorney general, was first elected governor in 2024, succeeding fellow Republican Gov. Chris Sununu. New Hampshire and neighboring Vermont are the only states in the nation that elect their governors every two years. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Ayotte started the cycle as the favorite due in part to political history. Only twice in the past century — and not since 2004 — have first-term New Hampshire governors been ousted. The governor highlighted affordable housing as her state's most pressing economic challenge, and she pointed to new laws on accessory dwelling units and permitting to help ease the crisis. DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB Warmington, a healthcare attorney and former member of New Hampshire's five-member elected executive council, which approves state contracts and the governor's judicial and executive branch nominations, highlighted the cost of living as she ran for governor. She called for a suspension of the state's gas tax. The Democratic nominee's past work as a lobbyist for drugmaker Purdue Pharma was a major line of attack by Ayotte, and the governor and her campaign labeled Warmington an "opioid lobbyist." "Kelly Ayotte is spending millions of dollars attacking me for work I did decades ago and regret. That’s so you won’t look at what Kelly’s doing right now as governor," Warmington said in response. articles.title: The historic firsts of Election Day 2026, from Atlanta to Capitol Hill
articles.summary: Several candidates ranging from Keisha Lance Bottoms, Deb Haaland, Chris Pappas and Byron Donalds all make history on Election Day.
articles.body:
In a day of historic firsts, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia will become the nation's first Black woman governor, and Hakeem Jeffries is in line to be the first Black Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives, due to Democrats' dramatic wave of victories Nov. 3.

Texas Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinajosa is projected to become the first Hispanic governor of the Lone Star state, and the first Democratic governor in more than three decades.

Fellow Democrat Deb Haaland of New Mexico is also projected to win that state's governor race, which would make her the first Native American woman to serve as a governor of any state. She previously made history as the first Native American woman in Congress and the first Native American woman in the Biden administration cabinet.

Haaland is an enrolled member of the Pueblo of Laguna. She also has Jemez Pueblo heritage.

The Democratic nominee for Senate in Minnesota, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, is likely to win the Senate race in that blue-leaning state and become the first Native American woman in the Senate.

Flanagan, a member of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe, might be joined in the historic moment in the Senate by Yup'ik Alaska Native and former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola, D-Alaska, if she ousts incumbent Alaska GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan. However, Alaska's results could take up to two weeks to be reported.

Illinois will make history as the first state to have two women of color serving simultaneously in the U.S. Senate. Democratic Lt. Gov. Julianna Stratton defeated Republican challenger Don Tracy on Nov. 3. Stratton, who is Black and the heavy favorite, will join Sen. Tammy Duckworth, who is Asian American.

"All across the board, we're seeing history being made with the statements made by these accomplished women," National Urban League President and CEO Marc Morial told USA TODAY. "There might be more to come."

Bottoms, the former Atlanta mayor, was the second Black woman to run for Georgia governor after former Georgia State Rep. Stacey Abrams lost in both 2018 and 2022 as the Democratic nominee.

Hakeem Jeffries poised to be first Black speaker of the House

Additionally, Hakeem Jeffries will become the first Black speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives after Democrats were projected to win control of the chamber.

The New York lawmaker is now fast-tracked to the position that follows the vice president in the line of presidential succession, as well as leading a revitalized Democratic Party during President Donald Trump 's final two years in the White House.

"America is alive and well," Jeffries said in a late Election Day post on X .

Rep. Chris Pappas wins, becomes first openly gay male senator

Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas will become the first openly gay man to serve in the U.S. Senate after defeating former Republican Sen. John E. Sununu for New Hampshire's open Senate seat.

Pappas, a popular Democrat who has consistently won the historically purple 1st Congressional District, faced a serious challenge in Sununu , one of the more popular political families in the state, as polls had shown a single-digit contest throughout the campaign.

Pappas' victory holds a crucial Senate seat for Democrats as they hope to take the Senate majority. The seat was open after Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen's retirement.

Byron Donalds becomes Florida's first Black governor

Republican U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds also made history by becoming Florida's first Black governor.

The favored Donalds defeated Democrat David Jolly. Donalds' win marked the first time in eight years Floridians have picked a new governor to replace soon-to-be termed-out Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis.

Donalds received President Donald Trump's endorsement, but briefly distanced himself from the president as Trump's approval ratings hit new lows. On the campaign trail, Donalds said making Florida more affordable, lowering prescription prices, cutting taxes and insurance rates, and driving down housing costs were among his top priorities.

In addition to making history, Donalds' win continues the trend of Republicans winning every gubernatorial election in the Sunshine State since 1998.

David Crowley becomes Wisconsin's first Black governor

In Wisconsin, Milwaukee County Executive and Democrat David Crowley defeated Republican Tom Tiffany to become the state's first Black governor in an odds-defying run that included suspending his campaign just four months ago and being massively outspent by the GOP.

Crowley will also be only the third governor to be born in Milwaukee, the state's largest city. At age 40, Crowley will be the youngest Wisconsin governor in almost a century.

"Thank you for placing your faith in me. That's ultimately what voting is. A tremendous act of faith," Crowley said at a campaign event in Milwaukee. "Not faith in one person or party, but faith in the ideas and the lessons learned − that the right leadership can make a difference in people's lives."

articles.title: Longtime Dem Sen who lost his seat 2 years ago projected to secure comeback victory in midterm battleground
articles.summary: Former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown defeats Jon Husted in Ohio's special election, reclaiming the seat he lost to Bernie Moreno two years ago.
articles.body: Former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown is projected to win his bid to return to the U.S. Senate, defeating Republican Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio just two years after losing his seat to Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno, the Fox News Decision Desk projects. Brown’s victory marks a remarkable political comeback for the longtime Ohio Democrat, who served in the Senate from 2007 until 2025 before Moreno ousted him in one of the most closely watched races of the 2024 election. The Democrat will return to Washington after defeating Husted in a special election to serve the remainder of the term originally won by Vice President JD Vance. Husted was appointed to the seat by Republican Gov. Mike DeWine in January 2025 after Vance resigned from the Senate to serve as President Donald Trump's No. 2. Brown previously represented Ohio in the U.S. House and served as the state’s secretary of state and a member of the Ohio House. THE NINE KEY RACES THAT WILL DECIDE WHO CONTROLS THE SENATE, AND WHERE THEY STAND The timing of Brown’s return to Washington will depend on when Ohio certifies the election and when he is formally sworn in. Brown could be sworn in during the lame-duck session, potentially changing the Senate’s voting math before the new Congress convenes. The Ohio race was viewed as a key battleground because Democrats saw the state as one of their best opportunities to erode the GOP’s narrow Senate majority, while Republicans viewed Husted’s seat as critical to maintaining control of the chamber. FOX NEWS POLL: ECONOMIC ANXIETY AND CANDIDATE CONCERNS DEFINE OHIO SENATE RACE Brown’s win came two years after he lost his Senate seat to Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno, as Ohio continued its shift toward the GOP in presidential elections. Former President Donald Trump carried the state by 11 percentage points in 2024, and Republicans argued that Brown’s return would amount to a restoration of the Democratic establishment that Ohio voters had rejected. Brown sought to overcome those headwinds by emphasizing his record on manufacturing, organized labor, trade, consumer protections and economic issues. His campaign focused heavily on the cost of living, gas and diesel prices, health care and the impact of Republican policies on working-class Ohioans. The candidates also clashed over data centers and energy costs. Brown criticized Husted’s role in supporting major economic development projects involving data centers, arguing that Ohio taxpayers and consumers could be left responsible for the infrastructure and energy demands associated with the facilities. Husted defended the projects as a way to bring jobs and investment to Ohio. He also pointed to legislation aimed at preventing taxpayers from bearing the operating costs of large data centers which Democrats blocked in the Senate. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Husted, a longtime figure in Ohio Republican politics, campaigned on his record as the state’s lieutenant governor, secretary of state and House speaker. He argued that Brown would return to Washington as a reliable vote for Senate Democrats and national party leaders. Brown's victory gives Democrats a huge boost in their bid to take back control of the United States Senate when the votes are all counted after Election Day.

articles.title: Democratic Party wins US Senate in 2026 midterm elections
articles.summary: The outcome is widely seen as a rebuke to Trump’s Republican Party, which won control of the chamber in 2024.
articles.body:
The Democratic Party has regained control of the upper chamber of the United States Congress in the 2026 midterm elections, according to Associated Press news agency projections.

The Senate was called in the party’s favour late on Tuesday night, marking a dramatic shift in legislative power.

Democrats needed a net gain of four seats in the 100-member chamber to wrest control from the Republicans. As of late Tuesday night, they had wrested control of at least seven seats.

Some of those gains were dramatic. In South Carolina, for instance, Democrat Annie Andrews, a paediatrician, took a seat held by Republican Darline Graham, the sister of the late longtime Senator Lindsey Graham. The last time a Democrat won a Senate seat in the state was 1998.

Neighbouring North Carolina saw a similar flip, with Democrat Roy Cooper, a former governor, beating his Republican rival Michael Whatley.

In Texas, a Republican stronghold, Democrat James Talarico, a state legislator and seminary student, delivered an upset against state Attorney General Ken Paxton. The last time a Democrat won a statewide election in Texas was 1994.

Democrat Sherrod Brown also defeated incumbent Republican Senator Jon Husted in Ohio, flipping that seat as well. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton, the Democratic pastor of a megachurch, beat another sitting senator, Republican Roger Marshall. In Maine, Democrat Troy Jackson unseated longtime Republican incumbent Senator Susan Collins. And in Iowa, paralympic gold medalist Josh Turek defeated Republican Ashley Hinson in a race that drew hundreds of millions of dollars in ad spending.

In the outgoing 119th Congress, Republicans hold a 53-seat majority. The Democrats have 45 seats, with two independents in their caucus.

With Tuesday’s results, Democrats have secured at least 53 seats, enough to take the majority, with a handful of races still being counted.

The outcome is also set to end the Republican “trifecta” achieved in the 2024 election, when the party won control of the three main levers of power in Washington, DC: the Senate, the House of Representatives and the presidency.

US President Donald Trump acknowledged the Democrats “did a good job” and had “fought hard” in the elections. Speaking to Fox News, he said he thought the war on Iran played a role in the Republican losses, as voters probably weren’t ready for “the short-term consequence of paying more for gasoline”.

But in a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump distanced himself from the results, saying “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”.

The Senate was projected to be harder to flip than the House in Tuesday’s midterm elections, given the smaller number of seats on the ballot.

Senate terms last six years, unlike the two-year terms of members of the House of Representatives. And elections for senators are staggered, meaning that only about a third of all Senate seats are voted on at a time.

This midterm election cycle saw 35 Senate races: 33 regular elections and two special elections, in Ohio and Florida. Those two states were left with Senate vacancies when Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio joined President Donald Trump’s second administration in 2025.

At least seven Senate races on Tuesday were considered key toss-ups. They included contests in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Ohio, Texas and Michigan.

States like Texas and Kansas, however, rarely fall within the toss-up category, as they are considered Republican strongholds. The last time a Democratic senator was elected in Kansas was 1932.

“How did this happen? How did a Democrat win in Kansas, a deeply red state, for the first time in nearly a century, especially in a state where only 25 percent of the people are Democrats?” Senator-elect Hamilton said in his victory speech.

“First of all, I think the people in Kansas – Republicans, independents and Democrats – were saying what’s happening in Washington is not OK.”

The Democratic Party also successfully defended several seats, including Jon Ossoff’s in the swing state of Georgia. Mark Warner, who has represented Virginia in the Senate since 2009, won a fourth term.

Trump said he would work with Democrats in the next Congress, even though he expected them to propose legislation he called “insane”.

“They’ll send over things that are insane, and I’ll veto them,” ⁠said Trump. “And after a couple ⁠of months of vetoes, they’ll call and they’ll say, ‘How do we get this stuff done?’ ⁠And we’ll work together.”

articles.title: The lawmaker who led Republican efforts to keep the House loses his re-election bid
articles.summary: Rep. Richard Hudson, R-N.C., lost to Democrat Richard Ojeda in North Carolina’s 9th District, NBC News projected.
articles.body: Rep. Richard Hudson, R-N.C., chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee, lost his re-election bid Tuesday, NBC News projected. Hudson fell short to Democrat Richard Ojeda in North Carolina’s 9th Congressional District. Ojeda bested Hudson by about 2 percentage points. Republicans have held the district since 1963. The National Republican Congressional Committee is the official party organization tasked with winning or maintaining the House majority. Hudson is the second party campaign chairman to lose re-election in the last two midterm cycles. In 2022, then-Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee chairman, lost his re-election bid in New York’s 17th District. Hudson was defeated after Republicans largely stopped investing in North Carolina’s high-profile Senate contest with weeks to go after Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper built a seemingly insurmountable advantage over Republican Michael Whatley, Trump’s handpicked candidate who was previously Republican National Committee chairman and head of the North Carolina state GOP. As of 10 p.m. Tuesday, Cooper, whom NBC News projected as the victor, led Whatley by nearly 20 points, boosting multiple downballot Democrats.

articles.title: Democrat Josh Turek flips Iowa Senate seat
articles.summary: Turek beat Republican Ashley Hinson, a US House member.
articles.body:
Democrat Josh Turek has been elected to the US Senate, defeating Republican Representative Ashley Hinson.

Turek’s victory over Hinson flips a Republican-held seat and boosts Democrats’ efforts to retake control of the Senate.

A state representative since 2023, Turek competed in four Paralympics and played professional wheelchair basketball in Europe.

Hinson was endorsed by Trump, who carried Iowa ⁠in three straight presidential elections. Turek’s victory underscored Democratic gains in a state that had initially been expected to remain safely Republican.

It’s been more than a decade since a Democrat represented Iowa in the Senate. The seat is held by retiring two-term Senator Joni Ernst.

articles.title: Florida Republicans fend off Democrats as state elects first black governor
articles.summary: Republican Byron Donalds, who was backed by President Donald Trump, will be the first black governor of Florida.
articles.body:
Republican candidates in Florida have held off several high-profile challenges from Democrats, as results also saw the state elect its first black governor.

Republican Byron Donalds, backed by President Donald Trump, was projected to win as governor, while Republican Ashley Moody was projected to have held her seat in the senate.

She was up against Democrat Angie Nixon in the special election for Secretary of State Marco Rubio's old Senate seat.

The two wins came amid countless - and historic - gains by Democrats that gave them full control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate for the last years of Trump's presidency.

Nixon scored a surprise win in the Democratic primary to become her party's standard-bearer, although her campaign funding could not match Moody's.

Donalds had served in Congress since 2021 before running for governor, to replace long-serving Republican Governor Ron DeSantis, who was term limited and could not run again.

A big supporter of Trump, Donalds was at one point on the short list to be his running mate in 2024.

Born in Brooklyn, he moved to Florida for university and became a fixture in local politics before running for Congress.

Democrats in the state had some surprise wins, too. Republicans in Florida had helped redraw political voting maps as part of a national redistricting push to boost each political party's chances of taking seats in the House.

But in all three districts that were redrawn to help Republicans, Democrats held onto their seats.

articles.title: Sen. Amy Klobuchar wins the Minnesota governor’s race, extending Democrats’ hold on the state
articles.summary: NBC News projects that Klobuchar has defeated GOP state House Speaker Lisa Demuth to become the first female governor in Minnesota’s history.
articles.body: Sen. Amy Klobuchar has won the Minnesota governor’s race, NBC News projects, a victory that will make her the first woman to lead the Midwestern state. Klobuchar, 66, defeated Republican Lisa Demuth, the state House speaker, extending the Democratic Party’s grip on the governor’s mansion. Minnesota has not elected a Republican governor since 2006. Although the national political environment favored Democrats this year, the party’s brand in the state has been tarnished in recent years. Two-term Gov. Tim Walz, the Democratic vice presidential nominee in 2024, faced intense scrutiny over the state’s handling of daycare fraud allegations. Walz abandoned his bid for a third term in early January, later vowing he would “never run for an elected office again.” Klobuchar then jumped into the Democratic gubernatorial primary and went on to easily win the nomination. In launching her campaign for governor, Klobuchar pledged to be a bulwark against President Donald Trump, whose administration deployed federal immigration officers to Minnesota this year as part of a sweeping crackdown that some residents likened to an “invasion.” “Minnesota, we’ve been through a lot,” Klobuchar said, referring to the fatal shootings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by U.S. immigration agents, as well as the assassinations last year of former state House Speaker Melissa Hortman and her husband. “These times call for leaders who can stand up and not be rubber stamps for this administration but who are also willing to find common ground and fix things in our state,” Klobuchar said. “These times call for grit and resilience.” She also nodded to the social services scandals that have roiled Minnesota, pledging to take a hard line against any abuse of public money. “I will make sure the people who steal taxpayer money go to jail and root out the fraud by changing the way state government works,” she said. “I will do my job without fear or favor. I’ve never shied away from taking on the powerful.” Klobuchar started her career in public office as Hennepin County’s top prosecutor. She was elected to the U.S. Senate in 2006, making her the state’s first woman to be elected to the chamber. She comfortably won re-election in 2012, 2018 and 2024. Klobuchar also unsuccessfully sought the Democratic presidential nomination in 2020.

articles.title: DOUG SCHOEN: The biggest winner and the biggest loser in the 2026 midterms
articles.summary: The Democratic Party swept formerly deep-red Senate seats in South Carolina, Kansas and Texas. What we've just witnessed is a collapse of the Republican Party.
articles.body: The big winner in the midterms on Tuesday night was the Democratic Party. And the big loser of the 2026 midterms was President Donald J. Trump. It’s impossible not to draw that conclusion given the blowout victory the Democrats won in both the House and Senate on Tuesday. While some races remain to be called, it is clear that the Democrats will have solid majorities in both houses of Congress, including winning Senate seats in formerly deep-red states like South Carolina, Kansas and Texas, which were considered, earlier in the year, virtually unachievable for Democrats. But make no mistake, this is more of a collapse of the Republican Party than it is an affirmative vote for the Democrats. This is a vote against the war in Iran as it’s being conducted, against high gas prices — which are seen as a direct result of that war — and against the overall perception among voters that there are two sets of rules for how government works: one for the rich and elites and another for ordinary working people. POWER SHIFT: FOX NEWS DECISION DESK PROJECTS DEMOCRATS WIN BACK SENATE, ENDING GOP CONTROL What remains unknown is whether the Democrats, having elected a number of progressives like James Talarico in Texas, and Troy Jackson in Maine, will be able to govern coherently and consistently in the Senate, and to a lesser extent in the House, with an agenda that is sympathetic to or actually aligned with the democratic socialists. Will these Democrats be able to coherently address the challenges that the Republicans and Trump have been unable to address in the last two years? Make no mistake, Tuesday’s results signal a collapse of the Republican Party more than an affirmative vote for the Democrats. The fear is great that the way Democrats will paper over these profound differences between their establishment wing and their far-left progressive wing will be not with policy but with investigations. And if that is the case, the degree of paralysis we’ve already seen in the last two years in Congress will only become a more stark reality. Voters are making it abundantly clear that President Trump’s approach of simply demonizing the opposition is not an acceptable or appropriate way to govern. That is why he is the biggest loser of Tuesday night, and it’s also why the Democrats are the biggest winners. The message to both parties is clear: Govern constructively, and if you don’t, it’s at your peril. The same swing against the Republicans we’ve just witnessed can happen in two short years to Democrats if they do not heed this judgment.
