articles.title: Trump-backed ex-NFL reporter loses Senate race to progressive who vowed to 'rip ICE apart'
articles.summary: Peggy Flanagan defeated Michele Tafoya in Minnesota's special election after ICE's Operation Metro Surge became a central rallying cry for her campaign.
articles.body: Progressives scored a major victory in Minnesota, a state heavily targeted by the Trump administration in its immigration and anti-fraud crackdowns. Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, the Democratic nominee, toppled former NFL sideline reporter and Republican nominee Michele Tafoya, stifling the GOP’s hopes of flipping the Land of 10,000 Lakes. While her win over Tafoya, who was backed by President Donald Trump, is a positive for Democrats in their pursuit of power in the upper chamber, it's not necessarily a negative for Republicans, given that the seat was already blue. PEGGY FLANAGAN VOWS TO 'RIP ICE APART' AFTER TOPPLING MODERATE DEM IN KEY SENATE BATTLE Flanagan’s victory comes after the state of Minnesota and her former running mate, Gov. Tim Walz, were directly in the Trump administration’s crosshairs for the sprawling, multibillion-dollar daycare fraud scandal that erupted earlier this year. Given that several Somali immigrants were linked to the scandal, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) descended upon the state to enact Operation Metro Surge. That resulted in the deaths of two Minnesota residents, Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti, at the hands of federal immigration agents. ICE’s actions in the state led to yet another government shutdown in Washington, D.C., and became a pointed rallying cry for her campaign and ammunition she used on the trail. MN SENATE CANDIDATE RIPPED FOR BLAMING WALZ FOR FRAUD DESPITE BEING HIS #2: 'KNOWS SHE'S COOKED' "We need to rip ICE apart and stop them from terrorizing our communities," Flanagan said shortly after winning her primary earlier this year. "And I know this. I know that we can fix our broken immigration system, secure the border, and create a real pathway to citizenship that aligns with our values." Much of Tafoya’s campaign hinged on what role Flanagan played in the Minnesota fraud scheme and just how much she knew as a top official in the state. "My opponent has been second in command in this state for eight years, drawing a taxpayer-funded paycheck," Tafoya said at a debate last month. "And what do we have to show for that? We have massive fraud, historic fraud. We have test scores down. We have crime spiking. We have a massive surplus turned into a deficit." SLEEPER GOP CANDIDATE PUTS BLUE-LEANING STATE IN PLAY AS FRAUD SCANDAL SHADOWS DEMS Flanagan, however, has shifted much of the blame for the scandal onto Walz and countered that "he was the one who had oversight here." "The governor has been very clear that the buck stops with him," Flanagan said. Her win could also be a double-edged sword for Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and his ambition to stay on as leader of Senate Democrats. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Flanagan, like other progressive Democratic candidates, has actively run away from and criticized Schumer, arguing that Democrats need change at the leadership level. "People want big, bold change," Flanagan told The New York Times. "They are sick of nibbling around the edges."

articles.title: GOP Rep. Max Miller loses re-election in Ohio following abuse allegations from his ex-wife
articles.summary: Miller has denied the allegations, which featured prominently in the campaign. Democrat Brian Poindexter defeated the two-term congressman, NBC News projects.
articles.body: Ohio Democrat Brian Poindexter has defeated Republican Rep. Max Miller, NBC News projects, months after Miller’s ex-wife accused him of domestic abuse — allegations he denied but which became the centerpiece of the campaign. Poindexter, an ironworker and City Council member in the working-class Cleveland suburb of Brook Park, flipped a district that Donald Trump would have won by 11 points in 2024. Poindexter and his allies amplified the abuse allegations as Democrats poured millions into a race they weren’t expecting to compete in just months before. Miller, 37, spent Trump’s first term as a White House aide and campaign hand. He originally sought to challenge then-Rep. Anthony Gonzalez in a 2022 GOP primary with Trump’s blessing after Gonzalez backed Trump’s impeachment the previous year. Gonzalez ended up retiring instead of running for re-election, and Miller won a different seat after redistricting jumbled the state’s congressional map. During that campaign, former White House press secretary Stephanie Grisham accused Miller of physical abuse while they were dating, allegations Miller denied. In Congress, Miller remained a steadfast ally of Trump, but he did break from him over some issues, like his tariffs, and he was also steadfast in his support for Ukraine in its war against Russia. Miller made headlines for taking on progressive Democrats over their support for Palestinians amid Israel’s war against Hamas in Gaza, and he backed the expulsion of Republican Rep. George Santos from Congress, accusing Santos of stealing money from him and his mother. Miller had been expected to win re-election easily until the circumstances surrounding his divorce became public. His ex-wife, Emily Moreno, has accused him of holding a gun to her head, throwing hot water on her and throwing her against a wall, allegations that have been aired both in courtrooms and in public. Miller has vehemently denied the claims. Miller released a series of documents and audio recordings of conversations between him and Moreno. He also defended himself in a lengthy social media livestream. “Ask yourself: If I had assaulted her, would she have offered to cook me dinner six days later?” he said in the social media video released this summer. “Would she have invited me to spend an afternoon at the playground with her and our daughter? Would she have written that we were in a friendlier place?” Moreno’s spokesperson Stefan Mychajliw called the video “unhinged and humiliating,” calling Miller’s denial of the allegations a lie and saying Moreno is “confident that justice will prevail in court.” Miller’s ex-wife is the daughter of Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, who spoke out over the summer, saying that he had hoped to not publicly weigh in “out of concern for the safety for my family” but that he felt that “Miller’s increasingly erratic and dangerous behavior has made that impossible.” The senator went on to say, “If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them,” and he said Miller “should not serve in the House of Representatives.” Despite calls from the senator and some other Republicans to resign before the deadline passed to replace him on the ballot, Miller was undeterred. Meanwhile, Poindexter suddenly found himself at the center of one of the most competitive House races in the country. He brought together backers including progressives like Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., who endorsed him ahead of his primary victory over longtime Ohio Democrat Ed FitzGerald. After the primary, Poindexter won the backing of other Democrats, like Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona, as the party sought to unite behind his campaign. After having voted Republican in his 20s, Poindexter began identifying more with Democrats, supporting President Barack Obama’s 2012 re-election and finding inspiration in Sanders’ 2016 presidential bid. On top of the attacks on Miller, Poindexter has leaned into a populist message highlighting his union background and promising to advocate for workers in Congress. While he has said he disagrees with Trump’s blanket tariffs, Poindexter backed “targeted tariffs to protect jobs” and argued for ways to rebuild America’s manufacturing sector. He also told the Akron Beacon Journal he supports “working towards universal health care over time” and working to protect union rights. As Poindexter and his allies hammered Miller, Republicans unspooled their own lines of attack against Poindexter, highlighting his past arrests. As a young adult, Poindexter faced a handful of criminal charges. He told NBC News this summer that his 1999 felonious assault charge was reduced to a misdemeanor, and he was charged in 2002 and 2003 with misdemeanor disorderly conduct related to fights at Cleveland Browns games. He added in his NBC News interview that he turned over a new leaf after he became a father at 22. “I was young and dumb, but I turned my life around. That was 25 years ago. But Max Miller, even after at least three women have accused Miller of violence and brutality, all Miller does is attack and lie,” Poindexter said in a TV ad.

articles.title: GOP senator's 30-year reign ends as 5th-generation logger pulls off stunning upset
articles.summary: Troy Jackson's upset over Susan Collins ends her nearly three-decade Senate career and hands Democrats a critical pickup in the 2026 midterms.
articles.body: Fifth-generation logger Troy Jackson has pulled off a major upset in Maine, defeating incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins and giving the Democratic Party a major boost in the battle for the U.S. Senate, the Fox News Decision Desk projects. Jackson's victory will end Collins’ nearly three-decade career in the Senate. "Maine, I owe you everything," Jackson wrote on X. "I’m ready to get to work for Mainers in the U.S. Senate, and I promise you this: I’ll never forget where I came from or who I’m fighting for." The win gives Democrats a major pickup in one of the most closely watched races of the 2026 midterm elections. The Maine contest was viewed as a critical test of whether Democrats could defeat a Republican incumbent in a state that has shifted increasingly toward the party in recent presidential elections. The result also could have major implications for control of the Senate. SCHUMER WARNS OF REPUBLICAN ADVANTAGE THAT COULD CHANGE THE BATTLE FOR SENATE CONTROL "It has been the honor of my life to serve the people of Maine in the United States Senate. I'm proud of all I have been able to accomplish for our state and for our country in the past 30 years," Collins wrote in conceding the race to her Democrat challenger. "I called Troy Jackson tonight to congratulate him and to assure him that my staff and I will work to ensure a smooth transition." Jackson previously served as president of the Maine Senate and represented parts of Aroostook County in the state Legislature. He campaigned as a working-class Democrat and labor advocate who would challenge both Washington’s political establishment and wealthy interests after he replaced disgraced Senate nominee Graham Platner on the ballot. Platner dropped out of the race in July amid allegations of sexual assault, which prompted a vote within the Maine Democratic Party to install Jackson. Jackson's campaign was nearly knocked off its tracks early on when it was revealed his longtime partner and mother of his two children is also his second cousin — the two share great-grandparents, according to reports. But that scandal wasn't enough to stop him from toppling the political institution that is Senator Collins. COLLINS INSISTS SOCIALIST RIVAL WON'T BEAT HER AS MAINE'S MONEY MACHINE: 'YOU'LL LOSE BIG TIME' Collins, who was first elected to the U.S. Senate in 1996, was seeking a sixth term. She is Maine’s longest-serving member of Congress and chaired the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee, a position that gave her significant influence over federal spending and funding for Maine projects. Collins, one of the more moderate Republicans in the Senate, built her latest reelection campaign around her reputation for independence and bipartisan dealmaking. She highlighted her work on infrastructure, veterans’ issues, rural communities and federal assistance for Maine residents while arguing that her seniority and committee position gave the state an advantage in Washington. The race was shaped by Collins’ complicated relationship with President Donald Trump and the Republican Party. Democrats criticized Collins over her votes for Trump-backed policies and her vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, arguing that her reputation as a moderate no longer matched her voting record. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Collins countered by pointing to the times she opposed Trump and Senate Republicans. She emphasized her willingness to break with her party and argued that Maine voters valued her independence more than party loyalty. "Troy and Chuck Schumer and their allies run ads saying that I'm somehow a puppet of the president. Believe me, that would come as a huge surprise to President Trump," the senator said in an interview last month with Fox News Digital. Former Democratic Sen. Joe Manchin campaigned with Collins in the closing weeks of the race, helping her make the case that she was a bipartisan senator who could work with lawmakers from both parties. Jackson’s victory marks a significant political shift in Maine and ends Collins’ run as one of the Republican Party’s most durable statewide candidates. Collins won reelection by nearly nine percentage points in 2020, but Democrats entered the 2026 contest with advantages driven by the state’s increasingly Democratic electorate and opposition to the Trump administration. Jackson will enter the Senate as a former state legislative leader with strong ties to organized labor and rural Maine. His election is likely to make him a prominent voice on economic issues as Democrats seek to appeal to working-class voters across the country.

articles.title: ‘LAWYER UP’: Dems immediately put Trump on notice amid Republicans' midterm bloodbath
articles.summary: Democrats on Capitol Hill warned the Trump administration to "lawyer up" as they prepare subpoenas and investigations targeting Pete Hegseth and others.
articles.body: Democrats wasted little time putting the Trump administration on notice after their sweeping midterm victories, firing off blunt warnings of subpoenas and investigations as they prepared to wield newfound power on Capitol Hill. "LAWYER UP," Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., the top Democrat on the powerful House Oversight Committee, posted on X. Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., offered an even more succinct preview of what could be ahead with the signle word post: "Subpoenas." As election results rolled in Tuesday night the picture for the next two years became increasingly bleak for Republicans and President Donald Trump's agenda.. DEMOCRAT SEIZE HOUSE CONTROL IN STUNNING BLUE TSUNAMI, VOW RETRIBUTION AGAINST TRUMP ADMIN Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., rattled off a list of Trump administration officials and allies she appeared eager to haul before Congress. "Noem, Markwayne, Miller, Homan, Bovino, what’s up? Clear your schedule," Ramirez wrote. "They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing," Sen. Ed Markey, D-Conn. , wrote on X. The warnings offered an early glimpse of the investigations that could consume Washington when the new Congress convenes in January. Democrats are preparing to use committee gavels and subpoena power to scrutinize Trump and his administration after two years in the minority and little ability to move the needle at all. Democrats have spent months laying the groundwork for this moment, mapping out investigations and sending document requests that could be followed by subpoenas once they take control of congressional committees. KATHY HOCHUL 'EXCITED' ABOUT PROSPECT OF DEMOCRATS TYING TRUMP UP IN INVESTIGATIONS Garcia, who is in line to chair the House Oversight Committee, has said his panel would move quickly on investigations spanning the Trump family's business dealings, immigration enforcement, alleged corporate corruption and the handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files. "We’re not starting from scratch here," Garcia told Punchbowl News ahead of the election, saying his team had been quietly preparing for months. Garcia has also pointed to the tools that come with the majority — including subpoenas, contempt proceedings and the ability to take disputes to court — as Democrats prepare for likely resistance from the White House. The coming investigations are expected to extend well beyond the Oversight Committee. Democrats on the House Judiciary and Homeland Security committees have spent the past two years pressing the administration over immigration enforcement and other Trump policies, while Senate Democrats could use their newly won committee gavels to launch investigations of their own. War Secretary Pete Hegseth could face particularly intense scrutiny. Democrats had already introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth before taking the majority, accusing him of offenses ranging from waging an unauthorized war against Iran to obstructing congressional oversight. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries went further last month, declaring that "one of the first things" Democrats would do in the majority would be to "run Pete Hegseth out of town." Hegseth could face a reckoning even sooner considering Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., has said he plans to force a vote on his own resolution to impeach the secretary when lawmakers return for the lame-duck session. He has accused Hegseth of violating the War Powers Resolution during the Iran war and acting unlawfully in U.S. military operations in Venezuela, Yemen and against suspected drug traffickers. Congressional committees have broad investigative powers, including the authority to subpoena administration officials and private citizens to testify under oath and compel them to turn over documents, communications and other records. Committee chairs can also wield significant power on their own. House rules allow committees to delegate subpoena authority to their chairs, meaning some incoming Democratic chairmen could issue demands for testimony or documents without first securing Republican support. Ignoring a congressional subpoena can trigger contempt proceedings, although forcing compliance — particularly from executive branch officials who invoke privilege — can lead to lengthy legal battles. Congress can pursue contempt of Congress or seek enforcement through the federal courts. Former Trump advisers Steve Bannon and Peter Navarro were both convicted of contempt of Congress after refusing to comply with subpoenas from the House committee investigating the Jan. 6 Capitol attack, and each was sentenced to four months in prison. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Congress can vote to hold a witness in criminal contempt and refer the matter to the Justice Department, which retains a role in deciding whether to pursue prosecution, a significant hurdle when Congress is seeking information from officials serving in the executive branch.

articles.title: Scandal-plagued Ilhan Omar easily secures 5th term in deep blue Minnesota despite immigration fraud probe
articles.summary: Ilhan Omar won reelection despite a federal probe into whether she committed immigration fraud, including claims she married her brother in 2009.
articles.body: MINNEAPOLIS — Despite an ongoing federal criminal probe that includes questions about her immigration status and another examining her financial disclosures, Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., cruised to reelection Tuesday night. Omar has represented Minnesota's 5th Congressional District, one of America's bluest, since winning in the 2018 midterms and becoming one of the first two Muslim women elected to the House of Representatives. The embattled, Somali-born congresswoman is projected to defeat Republican 30-year state trooper John Nagel. But after her election night victory, a potential fight looms on another front. ILHAN OMAR'S TURBULENT WEEK EXPLAINED: THE DUELING PROBES THAT THREW THE SOMALI-BORN PROGRESSIVE INTO CHAOS Omar's Washington, D.C., home was raided on Oct. 12, 2026, by agents with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the chief investigative body of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Fox News Digital first reported in the wake of the search that Omar is facing an investigation into whether she or her father lied on her immigration paperwork when applying for U.S. citizenship. HSI confiscated Omar's phone, passport and computer in the raid — investigators also obtained her DNA. Omar's sister, Sahra Noor, voluntarily spoke to federal investigators in the days after the raid, as reported by Fox News Digital. Court filings from the U.S. Attorney's Office in the District of Columbia referred to Omar as "Ilhan Omar Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Omar," suggesting that she shares a surname with the man she married in 2009. Ahmed Nur Said Elmi is a British citizen. Sources later told Fox News Digital that Ilhan Omar is not the Somali-born congresswoman's "real name." OBAMA ADMIN FIRST LAUNCHED THE INVESTIGATION INTO ILHAN OMAR'S ALLEGED BROTHER MARRIAGE That news renewed old claims that Ahmed Nur Said Elmi is the lawmaker's brother and that she married him in a potential immigration fraud scheme. A federal investigation into the matter was opened in 2016, and conducted by the FBI and DHS while former President Barack Obama was finishing out his second term. The investigation was eventually closed during former President Joe Biden's administration in 2021, a source told Fox News Digital. ILHAN OMAR FINALLY EMERGES AFTER DC RAID WITH VIDEO PLEADING FOR CASH TO FIGHT TRUMP Omar has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing, and she has not been charged with a crime. In several responses to inquiries about the investigation, she claimed President Donald Trump is orchestrating an attack against her for political purposes. "Trump has an unhealthy and creepy obsession with me," Omar told The Nation this week. "I represent everything Trump and today’s Republican Party seem to despise. I’m a woman, an immigrant, a refugee, a Muslim woman who wears a hijab, and someone who refuses to be intimidated into silence. I know who I am and why I do this work." "Rep. Omar has repeatedly and unequivocally denied this baseless, disgusting conspiracy theory," Omar's spokesperson Jackie Rogers told Fox News Digital upon the resurfacing of the alleged brother marriage claims. "This is a desperate political smear designed to distract from Trump’s failed presidency and two years of Republican failure in Congress. And it’s disgraceful that the media continues to give this lie oxygen." The raid on Omar's residence in the nation's capital that she shared with her current husband, political consultant Tim Mynett, took place in the final month of the midterm campaign. That didn't stop her from returning to her home state, reemerging to cast her ballot and convening with the Somali community at a Somali mall in Minneapolis. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP As the controversy built, Omar campaigned online and asked for donations from supporters to help her fight the costly battle she will likely face coming off of Tuesday's win. The week before the 2026 midterms, Omar embraced radical left-wing streamer Hasan Piker, who come to Minneapolis to campaign with the embattled lawmaker.

articles.title: Jocelyn Benson wins Michigan governor’s race, extending Democratic control
articles.summary: Benson will succeed Gretchen Whitmer, NBC News projects. It’s the first time in more than 60 years that Michigan will have had two Democratic governors in a row.
articles.body: Democrat Jocelyn Benson will be Michigan’s next governor, NBC News projects, succeeding term-limited Democrat Gretchen Whitmer to extend the party’s control for four more years. Benson, who is Michigan’s secretary of state, defeated Republican Rep. John James, who now finds himself without an elected office. It’s the first time since the 1960s that a Democrat will succeed a Democratic governor. Benson won as Michigan Democrats seek state legislative majorities to go with the governorship. The Democratic Party holds the state Senate but not the state House. Democrats would have to net four House seats and hold the Senate to secure full control of the state government. Democrats are also working to defend retiring Sen. Gary Peters’ seat, as Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers battle in a race that has drawn national attention. Donald Trump carried the state by a little over 1 percentage point in the 2024 presidential election. Benson, Michigan’s secretary of state since 2019, gained national prominence as the chief election officer for the battleground state as Trump tried to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election. Benson is an attorney who graduated from Harvard Law School and taught law at Wayne State University, where she went on to be dean. James was boosted by Trump, carrying him through his GOP primary. But he also sought to get some distance from Trump in the weeks leading up to the general election. James removed certain mentions of Trump from his campaign website, and at a debate in early October, he argued he would stand up to Trump on issues like the Iran war and tariffs on Canada, which have hit Michigan particularly hard. Benson criticized him for not voting for congressional resolutions to end the war. The two also sparred over data centers, with each saying the other profited from them. James accused Benson’s family of profiting from the construction of one data center, which she denied, while Benson said James had voted in favor of policies that favored data centers while he held stocks in them. James said any stocks related to data centers were held in broad mutual funds.
